Higher-tier understanding mechanisms coexist with lower-tier heuristics (e.g., memorization, n-gram statistics) within LLMs, impacting their epistemic trustworthiness.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often portrayed as merely imitating linguistic patterns without genuine understanding. We argue that recent findings in mechanistic interpretability (MI), the emerging field probing the inner workings of LLMs, render this picture increasingly untenable--but only once those findings are integrated within a theoretical account of understanding. We propose a tiered framework for thinking about understanding in LLMs and use it to synthesize the most relevant findings to date. The framework distinguishes three hierarchical varieties of understanding, each tied to a corresponding level of computational organization: conceptual understanding emerges when a model forms "features" as directions in latent space, learning connections between diverse manifestations of a single entity or property; state-of-the-world understanding emerges when a model learns contingent factual connections between features and dynamically tracks changes in the world; principled understanding emerges when a model ceases to rely on memorized facts and discovers a compact "circuit" connecting these facts. Across these tiers, MI uncovers internal organizations that can underwrite understanding-like unification. However, these also diverge from human cognition in their parallel exploitation of heterogeneous mechanisms. Fusing philosophical theory with mechanistic evidence thus allows us to transcend binary debates over whether AI understands, paving the way for a comparative, mechanistically grounded epistemology that explores how AI understanding aligns with--and diverges from--our own.

papers.title: Constructive Circuit Amplification: Improving Math Reasoning in LLMs via Targeted Sub-Network Updates
papers.research_question: How can we improve mathematical reasoning in LLMs by selectively updating the sparse subnetwork (circuit) responsible for correct reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Constructive Circuit Amplification (CCA), a method that improves mathematical reasoning in LLMs by identifying and updating only the sparse subnetwork (circuit) responsible for correct reasoning, achieving significant accuracy gains with minimal impact on other abilities.
papers.conclusion: CCA substantially improves mathematical reasoning across multiple model families while modifying a small fraction of components, with minimal degradation on general-purpose benchmarks, demonstrating that model capabilities are often governed by sparse, localized subnetworks that can be selectively strengthened.
papers.key_findings:
CCA improves mathematical reasoning accuracy by up to +11.4% on GSM-Symbolic across multiple models.
CCA modifies as little as 1.59% of model components (attention heads and MLP neurons).
CCA preserves general abilities (MMLU, TriviaQA, TruthfulQA) with minimal degradation.
The Branching method for token localization consistently outperforms the Prefix method.
CCA outperforms LoRA fine-tuning in some models and is effective in data-constrained settings.
papers.limitation:
Focused on mathematical reasoning, leaving open whether similar gains can be achieved for other complex domains such as code generation or scientific problem solving.
Requires constructing error-localization datasets for token localization, which may be costly in settings without well-defined correctness signals.
Experiments considered only a single fine-tuning stage, whereas deployed models often undergo multiple rounds of fine-tuning.
future_direction: Extending CCA to other capabilities and domains, such as code generation, scientific reasoning, or multi-modal tasks.
Automating the error-localization process using frontier LLMs to reduce reliance on multiple generations and improve scalability.
Incorporating more sophisticated optimization techniques to refine model components more efficiently than naive gradient descent.
papers.abstract: Prior studies investigating the internal workings of LLMs have uncovered sparse subnetworks, often referred to as circuits, that are responsible for performing specific tasks. Additionally, it has been shown that model performance improvement through fine-tuning often results from the strengthening of existing circuits in the model. Taken together, these findings suggest the possibility of intervening directly on such circuits to make precise, task-targeted updates. Motivated by these findings, we propose a novel method called Constructive Circuit Amplification which identifies pivotal tokens from model reasoning traces as well as model components responsible for the desired task, and updates only those components. Applied to mathematical reasoning, it improves accuracy by up to +11.4% across multiple models while modifying as little as 1.59% of model components, with minimal impact on other abilities as measured by MMLU, TriviaQA, and TruthfulQA. These results demonstrate that targeted capabilities can be reliably enhanced by selectively updating a sparse set of model components.

papers.title: The mechanistic basis of data dependence and abrupt learning in an in-context classification task
papers.research_question: What aspects of the training data distribution and architecture favor in-context vs in-weights learning, and what is the mechanistic basis of the abrupt transition observed during in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that data distributional dependencies for in-context learning are recapitulated in a minimal attention-only network, and that the abrupt transition in ICL is driven by the formation of an induction head, which is explained by a phenomenological model with nested logits.
papers.conclusion: The abrupt transition in ICL is due to the sequential learning of three nested logits in the induction head, and an intrinsic curriculum (slow learning of a simpler strategy) may be necessary to guide the network towards the ICL solution.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing burstiness (B) and number of classes (K) promotes ICL while decreasing IWL.
Within-class variation (ε) promotes ICL and decreases IWL.
A Zipfian rank-frequency distribution (α=1) promotes both ICL and IWL simultaneously.
The network can learn both ICL and IWL solutions simultaneously when trained on a mix of sequences.
The abrupt transition in ICL is driven by the formation of an induction head, preceded by a slow learning phase where the network learns to randomly pick a contextual label.
papers.limitation:
The model is minimal and larger models may use different mechanisms than the ones identified.
The analysis did not use heuristics such as weight tying, which are common in LLMs and might change the learning dynamics.
future_direction: Testing the hypothesis that learning of simpler ICL operations enables the learning of more complex ICL strategies in large language models.
Using methods for mechanistic interpretability to probe these mechanisms in LLMs.
Exploring the role of curricula for accelerating ICL in LLMs.
papers.abstract: Transformer models exhibit in-context learning: the ability to accurately predict the response to a novel query based on illustrative examples in the input sequence. In-context learning contrasts with traditional in-weights learning of query-output relationships. What aspects of the training data distribution and architecture favor in-context vs in-weights learning? Recent work has shown that specific distributional properties inherent in language, such as burstiness, large dictionaries and skewed rank-frequency distributions, control the trade-off or simultaneous appearance of these two forms of learning. We first show that these results are recapitulated in a minimal attention-only network trained on a simplified dataset. In-context learning (ICL) is driven by the abrupt emergence of an induction head, which subsequently competes with in-weights learning. By identifying progress measures that precede in-context learning and targeted experiments, we construct a two-parameter model of an induction head which emulates the full data distributional dependencies displayed by the attention-based network. A phenomenological model of induction head formation traces its abrupt emergence to the sequential learning of three nested logits enabled by an intrinsic curriculum. We propose that the sharp transitions in attention-based networks arise due to a specific chain of multi-layer operations necessary to achieve ICL, which is implemented by nested nonlinearities sequentially learned during training.

papers.title: PAHQ: Accelerating Automated Circuit Discovery through Mixed-Precision Inference Optimization
papers.research_question: How can automated circuit discovery be accelerated while maintaining faithfulness, addressing its computational inefficiency and high memory requirements?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PAHQ, a training-free mixed-precision quantization method that accelerates automated circuit discovery by maintaining high precision for critical attention heads and reducing precision elsewhere, achieving significant speedup and memory reduction with minimal faithfulness loss.
papers.conclusion: PAHQ provides an efficient acceleration approach for mechanistic interpretability research without sacrificing analytical quality, making circuit discovery more computationally feasible.
papers.key_findings:
PAHQ-accelerated ACDC reduces runtime by up to 80% and memory consumption by up to 30% compared to unaccelerated ACDC while maintaining faithfulness.
PAHQ outperforms RTN quantization and Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) in terms of AUC-ROC on circuit discovery tasks like IOI, Docstring, and Greater Than.
The method is training-free and readily integrates with existing edge-based circuit discovery techniques by modifying the attention computation mechanism.
PAHQ's selective precision allocation and three-stream parallel scheduler effectively mask data transfer latency, enabling near-optimal throughput.
The method scales effectively to larger transformer models (GPT-2-medium, large, XL) while maintaining competitive performance.
papers.limitation:
PAHQ is designed for algorithms that evaluate edges sequentially (like ACDC) and may not be as effective for methods that evaluate multiple edges simultaneously (like EAP).
PAHQ makes circuit discovery more feasible for moderately larger models but does not solve the scalability challenge for foundation models with hundreds of billions of parameters.
The method is empirically validated but lacks theoretical analysis on how high-precision signals propagate through lower-precision layers.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery, which involves identifying sparse and task-relevant subnetworks in pre-trained language models, is a cornerstone of mechanistic interpretability. Automated Circuit Discovery (ACDC) has emerged as a pivotal methodology in circuit discovery, but its application to large language models is severely limited by computational inefficiency and prohibitively high memory requirements. Although several accelerated approaches have been proposed, they primarily rely on linear approximations to ACDC, which significantly compromises analytical faithfulness. Our proposed method for accelerating automated circuit discovery, Per Attention Head Quantization (PAHQ), takes a fundamentally different approach by optimizing the efficiency of each individual patching operation. PAHQ leverages a fundamental alignment between activation patching and mixed-precision quantization (MPQ): interpretability analysis through patching essentially performs targeted ablation studies. Therefore, we can maintain high precision exclusively for investigated components while safely reducing precision elsewhere in the network. PAHQ-accelerated ACDC reduces runtime by up to 80\% and memory consumption by up to 30\% compared to unaccelerated ACDC while maintaining faithfulness. Importantly, our method readily integrates with existing edge-based circuit discovery techniques by modifying the attention computation mechanism. This training-free approach provides a practical and novel pathway for accelerating mechanistic interpretability methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/626619403/PAHQ.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability as Statistical Estimation: A Variance Analysis
papers.research_question: What is the stability of mechanistic interpretability methods, specifically circuit discovery, and how does variance in causal mediation analysis and its approximations affect the reliability of discovered circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that circuit discovery methods are highly unstable due to intrinsic variance in causal mediation analysis scores and amplification by approximation methods, advocating for more rigorous statistical practices in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Circuit discovery is not a stable process and requires statistical rigor, including reporting stability metrics and sensitivity analyses, to become a reliable scientific tool.
papers.key_findings:
Exact causal mediation analysis (CMA) scores exhibit high intrinsic variance across inputs, meaning the causal effect of a component is a volatile random variable.
Approximation methods like Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) amplify this variance, leading to low signal-to-noise ratios.
Circuit discovery pipelines are sensitive to data resampling, hyperparameters, and counterfactual definitions, resulting in structurally inconsistent circuits.
Larger models (e.g., Llama-3.2-1B) show higher variability in circuit discovery compared to smaller models (e.g., gpt2-small).
The instability of circuits is not mitigated by instruction tuning (comparing Llama-3.2-1B and its instruct variant).
papers.limitation:
Focus on the EAP family of methods, leaving out newer methods that may have different properties.
Exact CMA analysis was only done on gpt2-small for the IOI task due to computational constraints.
Limited to three classic MI tasks, which may not generalize to fuzzier reasoning tasks.
Stability metrics treat all edges equally, whereas weighted metrics might reveal a stable functional core.
future_direction: Probabilistic circuit discovery: characterizing a distribution over possible circuits.
Decomposing variance into estimator variance and intrinsic variance.
Stability-aware optimization: developing objectives that explicitly optimize for stability.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) aims to reverse-engineer model behaviors by identifying functional sub-networks. Yet, the scientific validity of these findings depends on their stability. In this work, we argue that circuit discovery is not a standalone task but a statistical estimation problem built upon causal mediation analysis (CMA). We uncover a fundamental instability at this base layer: exact, single-input CMA scores exhibit high intrinsic variance, implying that the causal effect of a component is a volatile random variable rather than a fixed property. We then demonstrate that circuit discovery pipelines inherit this variance and further amplify it. Fast approximation methods, such as Edge Attribution Patching and its successors, introduce additional estimation noise, while aggregating these noisy scores over datasets leads to fragile structural estimates. Consequently, small perturbations in input data or hyperparameters yield vastly different circuits. We systematically decompose these sources of variance and advocate for more rigorous MI practices, prioritizing statistical robustness and routine reporting of stability metrics.

papers.title: VISIT: Visualizing and Interpreting the Semantic Information Flow of Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we interpret and visualize the semantic information flow inside transformer language models, particularly focusing on attention heads and memory values?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a tool for visualizing the semantic information flow in transformer language models as an interactive flow graph, and provides new insights into layer norms as semantic filters and the existence of regularization neurons.
papers.conclusion: The work introduces a tool to visualize the semantic information flow in transformers using the logit lens, demonstrates its utility by revealing insights about layer norms and regularization neurons, and validates the approach by supporting other analyses.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads' semantics can be projected via the OV circuit, and only the heads with the largest norms dominate the block's output.
Memory values with the highest attention scores capture the semantics of their corresponding attention head.
Layer normalization layers act as semantic filters, demoting function words and promoting content words in the residual stream.
Regularization neurons exist that are consistently highly activated, have high entropy, and may serve as a constant bias or regularization term.
The flow-graph visualization tool can qualitatively replicate mechanistic analyses, such as indirect object identification, and reveal internal information flow patterns.
papers.limitation:
Limited to English language models, particularly GPT models with multi-head attention, and insights might not generalize to other languages or datasets.
Projection methods and the intersection score Ik have limitations in capturing semantic connections between different tokens with the same meaning.
Pruning based on the assumption that the most activated neurons determine the final prediction might be misleading as less activated neurons could also be relevant.
The methods are not causal and do not employ interventions, so further investigation is needed to fully understand the mechanisms.
future_direction: Apply causal interventions to verify the findings.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in interpretability suggest we can project weights and hidden states of transformer-based language models (LMs) to their vocabulary, a transformation that makes them more human interpretable. In this paper, we investigate LM attention heads and memory values, the vectors the models dynamically create and recall while processing a given input. By analyzing the tokens they represent through this projection, we identify patterns in the information flow inside the attention mechanism. Based on our discoveries, we create a tool to visualize a forward pass of Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPTs) as an interactive flow graph, with nodes representing neurons or hidden states and edges representing the interactions between them. Our visualization simplifies huge amounts of data into easy-to-read plots that can reflect the models' internal processing, uncovering the contribution of each component to the models' final prediction. Our visualization also unveils new insights about the role of layer norms as semantic filters that influence the models' output, and about neurons that are always activated during forward passes and act as regularization vectors.

papers.title: Comprehension Without Competence: Architectural Limits of LLMs in Symbolic Computation and Reasoning
papers.research_question: Why do Large Language Models (LLMs) systematically fail at tasks requiring symbolic reasoning, arithmetic accuracy, and logical consistency, despite being able to fluently explain the correct principles?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and analyzes a fundamental architectural limitation in LLMs termed the 'computational split-brain syndrome,' where models can explain principles they cannot reliably execute, due to geometric separation of instruction and execution pathways.
papers.conclusion: LLMs function as powerful pattern completion engines but lack the architectural scaffolding for principled, compositional reasoning, and fundamental architectural innovations are needed to overcome these limitations.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit a systematic gap between comprehension (explaining principles) and competence (executing them), termed computational split-brain syndrome.
This gap is rooted in architectural constraints: token embeddings resist domain binding, FFNs cannot implement exact symbolic operations, and next-token prediction decouples instruction from execution.
The syndrome manifests across domains (arithmetic and relational reasoning) and is not resolved by scaling or prompting.
Compensatory strategies (self-scaffolding, tool delegation, hybrid architectures) are necessary but highlight the need for metacognitive capabilities that current architectures lack.
Mechanistic interpretability findings may reflect training-specific pattern coordination rather than universal computational principles.
papers.limitation:
Focus on pretrained transformer-based LLMs without external tools or explicit reasoning scaffolds.
Empirical evaluation centers on specific model families (LLaMA2, Claude, GPT-4) and may not generalize to fundamentally different architectures.
Geometric separation experiments rely on t-SNE projections which may not capture all relevant representational structure.
Theoretical analysis of FFN computational limits focuses on ReLU networks and may not apply to other activation functions.
future_direction: Developing future models with metacognitive control, principle lifting, and structurally grounded execution.
Empirical validation of the hypothesis that similar constraints apply to architectural variations like mixture-of-experts.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) display striking surface fluency yet systematically fail at tasks requiring symbolic reasoning, arithmetic accuracy, and logical consistency. This paper offers a structural diagnosis of such failures, revealing a persistent gap between \textit{comprehension} and \textit{competence}. Through controlled experiments and architectural analysis, we demonstrate that LLMs often articulate correct principles without reliably applying them--a failure rooted not in knowledge access, but in computational execution. We term this phenomenon the computational \textit{split-brain syndrome}, where instruction and action pathways are geometrically and functionally dissociated. This core limitation recurs across domains, from mathematical operations to relational inferences, and explains why model behavior remains brittle even under idealized prompting. We argue that LLMs function as powerful pattern completion engines, but lack the architectural scaffolding for principled, compositional reasoning. Our findings delineate the boundary of current LLM capabilities and motivate future models with metacognitive control, principle lifting, and structurally grounded execution. This diagnosis also clarifies why mechanistic interpretability findings may reflect training-specific pattern coordination rather than universal computational principles, and why the geometric separation between instruction and execution pathways suggests limitations in neural introspection and mechanistic analysis.

papers.title: What needs to go right for an induction head? A mechanistic study of in-context learning circuits and their formation
papers.research_question: Why is there more than one induction head, and how are they dependent on each other? Why do induction heads appear all of a sudden, and what are the subcircuits that enable them to emerge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an artificial optogenetics framework for causal manipulation of activations during training and uses it to identify three interacting subcircuits that explain the phase change in induction head formation.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a deeper understanding of induction head formation and phase changes through the identification of subcircuits, and the introduced framework enables causal analysis of training dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Multiple induction heads form and contribute additively to minimize loss.
Induction heads and previous token heads are wired in a many-to-many fashion.
Three underlying subcircuits (match, copy, and routing) interact to drive the phase change in induction head formation.
The timing of the phase change depends on data properties, which can be understood through the subcircuits.
The network uses additional capacity (multiple heads) for faster training even when not strictly necessary.
papers.abstract: In-context learning is a powerful emergent ability in transformer models. Prior work in mechanistic interpretability has identified a circuit element that may be critical for in-context learning -- the induction head (IH), which performs a match-and-copy operation. During training of large transformers on natural language data, IHs emerge around the same time as a notable phase change in the loss. Despite the robust evidence for IHs and this interesting coincidence with the phase change, relatively little is known about the diversity and emergence dynamics of IHs. Why is there more than one IH, and how are they dependent on each other? Why do IHs appear all of a sudden, and what are the subcircuits that enable them to emerge? We answer these questions by studying IH emergence dynamics in a controlled setting by training on synthetic data. In doing so, we develop and share a novel optogenetics-inspired causal framework for modifying activations throughout training. Using this framework, we delineate the diverse and additive nature of IHs. By clamping subsets of activations throughout training, we then identify three underlying subcircuits that interact to drive IH formation, yielding the phase change. Furthermore, these subcircuits shed light on data-dependent properties of formation, such as phase change timing, already showing the promise of this more in-depth understanding of subcircuits that need to "go right" for an induction head.

papers.title: Attribution Patching Outperforms Automated Circuit Discovery
papers.research_question: Does a simple method based on attribution patching outperform existing automated circuit discovery methods in identifying circuits?
papers.core_contribution: Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) outperforms existing automated circuit discovery methods like ACDC in identifying circuits while being substantially faster, requiring only two forward passes and one backward pass.
papers.conclusion: Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) outperforms ACDC in identifying circuits and is faster, but its results can be improved by running ACDC on the pruned subgraph found by EAP.
papers.key_findings:
Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) has greater AUC for circuit recovery than ACDC on the IOI and Greater-Than tasks.
EAP is more efficient than activation patching, requiring only two forward passes and a backward pass.
The linear approximation of activation patching by attribution patching is not always accurate, especially when the task-specific metric is concave.
Running ACDC on the pruned subgraph returned by EAP can improve the identification of relevant edges.
Attribution scores for edges in the ground-truth circuit tend to be spread further from zero than edges not in the circuit.
papers.limitation:
The linear approximation used by attribution patching can be inaccurate, especially for edges from the model's embeddings, leading to overestimation of edge importance.
The metrics used for interpretability (e.g., circuit recovery against human-found circuits) do not precisely capture meaningful human understanding and are limited by the imperfections of human-found circuits.
future_direction: Future circuit discovery experiments should run EAP first and then apply ACDC on the pruned subgraph.

papers.title: Understanding In-Context Learning in Transformers and LLMs by Learning to Learn Discrete Functions
papers.research_question: What are the limits of in-context learning in Transformers, is attention necessary, can Transformers exploit teaching sequences for efficiency, and to what extent can LLMs implement learning algorithms from in-context examples?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that Transformers can implement near-optimal learning algorithms for simple Boolean functions, struggle with complex ones like parities, and can adaptively use teaching sequences for sample efficiency. Additionally, pretrained LLMs demonstrate non-trivial in-context learning abilities on discrete tasks.
papers.conclusion: The study advances understanding of in-context learning in Transformers and LLMs, showing their capabilities and limitations on discrete function learning, and highlights the potential for adaptive algorithm selection.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers achieve near-perfect accuracy on simple Boolean functions like conjunctions and disjunctions.
Transformers fail to learn parity functions effectively, performing no better than random guessing.
Attention-free models such as Hyena perform similarly to Transformers on most tasks, with minor gaps on some.
Transformers can learn from teaching sequences and implement sample-efficient algorithms, adapting based on input.
Pretrained LLMs like GPT-4 and LLaMA-2 can compete with nearest-neighbor baselines on Boolean function tasks not in their training set.
papers.limitation: Transformers fail to learn parity functions effectively, performing no better than random guessing.
papers.abstract: In order to understand the in-context learning phenomenon, recent works have adopted a stylized experimental framework and demonstrated that Transformers can learn gradient-based learning algorithms for various classes of real-valued functions. However, the limitations of Transformers in implementing learning algorithms, and their ability to learn other forms of algorithms are not well understood. Additionally, the degree to which these capabilities are confined to attention-based models is unclear. Furthermore, it remains to be seen whether the insights derived from these stylized settings can be extrapolated to pretrained Large Language Models (LLMs). In this work, we take a step towards answering these questions by demonstrating the following: (a) On a test-bed with a variety of Boolean function classes, we find that Transformers can nearly match the optimal learning algorithm for 'simpler' tasks, while their performance deteriorates on more 'complex' tasks. Additionally, we find that certain attention-free models perform (almost) identically to Transformers on a range of tasks. (b) When provided a teaching sequence, i.e. a set of examples that uniquely identifies a function in a class, we show that Transformers learn more sample-efficiently. Interestingly, our results show that Transformers can learn to implement two distinct algorithms to solve a single task, and can adaptively select the more sample-efficient algorithm depending on the sequence of in-context examples. (c) Lastly, we show that extant LLMs, e.g. LLaMA-2, GPT-4, can compete with nearest-neighbor baselines on prediction tasks that are guaranteed to not be in their training set.

papers.title: Physics Steering: Causal Control of Cross-Domain Concepts in a Physics Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Whether scientific foundation models learn abstract, domain-general representations of physical phenomena that can be causally manipulated via activation steering.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that a physics foundation model learns linearly steerable representations of physical concepts (e.g., vorticity, diffusion, temporal progression), and that injecting these directions during inference enables fine-grained causal control over simulation behavior. The concept directions are domain-general and transfer across unrelated physical systems.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability techniques from LLMs can be successfully adapted to scientific foundation models, providing evidence that these models develop abstract, domain-general representations of fundamental physical concepts that are linearly encoded and causally steerable.
papers.key_findings:
Single directions in the model's activation space correspond to specific physical concepts like vorticity, diffusion, and simulation speed.
Injecting (adding or subtracting) these concept directions during inference causally steers model predictions, allowing induction or suppression of vortices, enhancement or suppression of diffusion, and speeding up or slowing down simulations.
The extracted concept directions transfer successfully between unrelated physical systems (e.g., from fluid dynamics to chemical reaction-diffusion), indicating they represent abstract, domain-general physical principles.
The results support the Linear Representation Hypothesis for scientific foundation models, showing physical concepts are represented linearly in activation space.
Steering effects are more physically plausible and interpretable when using spatially-averaged concept directions that discard spatial structure, compared to using full spatial tensors.
papers.limitation:
The physical plausibility of the steered results is an open question; including spatial dimensions in the steering tensor can lead to less physically realistic outcomes.
The effectiveness of steering depends on the initial conditions of the simulation; steering becomes more difficult and can produce distorted fields when the initial state is far from the target regime.
future_direction: Exploring the layer-dependence of concept representations and steering effects.
Further work to definitively assess the physicality and self-consistency of steered simulation results.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have revealed that large language models (LLMs) develop internal representations corresponding not only to concrete entities but also distinct, human-understandable abstract concepts and behaviour. Moreover, these hidden features can be directly manipulated to steer model behaviour. However, it remains an open question whether this phenomenon is unique to models trained on inherently structured data (ie. language, images) or if it is a general property of foundation models. In this work, we investigate the internal representations of a large physics-focused foundation model. Inspired by recent work identifying single directions in activation space for complex behaviours in LLMs, we extract activation vectors from the model during forward passes over simulation datasets for different physical regimes. We then compute "delta" representations between the two regimes. These delta tensors act as concept directions in activation space, encoding specific physical features. By injecting these concept directions back into the model during inference, we can steer its predictions, demonstrating causal control over physical behaviours, such as inducing or removing some particular physical feature from a simulation. These results suggest that scientific foundation models learn generalised representations of physical principles. They do not merely rely on superficial correlations and patterns in the simulations. Our findings open new avenues for understanding and controlling scientific foundation models and has implications for AI-enabled scientific discovery.

papers.title: TX-Ray: Quantifying and Explaining Model-Knowledge Transfer in\n (Un-)Supervised NLP
papers.research_question: How can we explain and quantify model knowledge transfer during (un-)supervised training in NLP? Specifically, how do self-supervised models build knowledge abstractions during pretraining, what knowledge subset is applied in zero-shot transfer to a new domain, and how does knowledge transfer 'backwards' from supervision labels into a pretrained model?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces TX-Ray, a method that modifies activation maximization to represent neurons as feature preference distributions, enabling the analysis, tracking, and quantification of knowledge transfer and adaptation during pretraining, zero-shot application, and supervised fine-tuning in NLP models.
papers.conclusion: TX-Ray enables explorative analysis of how knowledge is lost and added during supervision, how neurons overfit or generalize, and how pretraining builds knowledge abstractions, providing a simple yet nuanced method for model knowledge explainability in transfer learning.
papers.key_findings:
TX-Ray can reveal how early stages of self-supervision automatically learn linguistic abstractions like parts-of-speech.
During zero-shot application, a pretrained encoder exhibits broad transfer, with 88.2% of neurons remaining 'shared' when applied to a new domain.
Supervision not only causes catastrophic forgetting but also adds new knowledge into previously unpreferred neurons.
TX-Ray-based pruning, similar to Lottery Ticket pruning, can improve test set generalization by removing 'avoided' neurons.
Supervision sparsifies neuron activations, leading to more peaked activation mass distributions compared to pretraining or zero-shot application.
future_direction: Use TX-Ray for more advanced transfer models and metrics.
papers.abstract:
While state-of-the-art NLP explainability (XAI) methods focus on explaining
per-sample decisions in supervised end or probing tasks, this is insufficient
to explain and quantify model knowledge transfer during (un-)supervised
training. Thus, for TX-Ray, we modify the established computer vision
explainability principle of 'visualizing preferred inputs of neurons' to make
it usable transfer analysis and NLP. This allows one to analyze, track and
quantify how self- or supervised NLP models first build knowledge abstractions
in pretraining (1), and then transfer these abstractions to a new domain (2),
or adapt them during supervised fine-tuning (3). TX-Ray expresses neurons as
feature preference distributions to quantify fine-grained knowledge transfer or
adaptation and guide human analysis. We find that, similar to Lottery Ticket
based pruning, TX-Ray based pruning can improve test set generalization and
that it can reveal how early stages of self-supervision automatically learn
linguistic abstractions like parts-of-speech.

papers.title: Representation in large language models
papers.research_question: Is LLM behavior driven partly by representation-based information processing of the sort implicated in biological cognition, or is it driven entirely by processes of memorization and stochastic table look-up?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that LLM behavior is partially driven by representation-based information processing, contrary to the look-up table view, and outlines how mechanistic interpretability methods can be used to study these representations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs do use representation-based information processing, and we can investigate these representations using mechanistic interpretability methods.
papers.key_findings:
The look-up table view of LLMs is inadequate because it cannot explain robust behavior.
Representations, as defined by four conditions (INFORMATION, EXPLOITABILITY, BEHAVIOR, ROLE), can explain robust behavior.
Mechanistic interpretability methods like probing and causal interventions can test for representations in LLMs.
papers.abstract: The extraordinary success of recent Large Language Models (LLMs) on a diverse array of tasks has led to an explosion of scientific and philosophical theorizing aimed at explaining how they do what they do. Unfortunately, disagreement over fundamental theoretical issues has led to stalemate, with entrenched camps of LLM optimists and pessimists often committed to very different views of how these systems work. Overcoming stalemate requires agreement on fundamental questions, and the goal of this paper is to address one such question, namely: is LLM behavior driven partly by representation-based information processing of the sort implicated in biological cognition, or is it driven entirely by processes of memorization and stochastic table look-up? This is a question about what kind of algorithm LLMs implement, and the answer carries serious implications for higher level questions about whether these systems have beliefs, intentions, concepts, knowledge, and understanding. I argue that LLM behavior is partially driven by representation-based information processing, and then I describe and defend a series of practical techniques for investigating these representations and developing explanations on their basis. The resulting account provides a groundwork for future theorizing about language models and their successors.

papers.title: Explaining the Explainer: Understanding the Inner Workings of Transformer-based Symbolic Regression Models
papers.research_question: How can we understand the internal mechanisms of transformer-based symbolic regression models, specifically by identifying circuits responsible for generating symbolic operators?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PATCHES, a novel evolutionary circuit discovery algorithm for symbolic regression transformers, and establishes a formal evaluation framework (faithfulness, completeness, minimality) for circuit correctness.
papers.conclusion: This work establishes symbolic regression as a promising domain for mechanistic interpretability and provides a principled methodology for circuit discovery in such models.
papers.key_findings:
PATCHES successfully isolates circuits for specific symbolic operators (e.g., sin, add, log) in a transformer-based SR model.
Mean patching combined with functional evaluation (accuracy) is more reliable for discovering correct circuits than resample patching or model-based (logit) evaluation.
Direct logit attribution and probing classifiers primarily capture correlational features, limiting their utility for causal circuit discovery.
Circuits for SR are dense (40-78% of model components), attributed to the small vocabulary and complex syntactic encoding required.
papers.limitation:
Resample patching sometimes fails to sufficiently suppress the target token's information, hindering causal isolation and circuit discovery.
High baseline performance for some operators (e.g., addition) makes it difficult to achieve completeness, as patching does not degrade performance enough.
papers.abstract: Following their success across many domains, transformers have also proven effective for symbolic regression (SR); however, the internal mechanisms underlying their generation of mathematical operators remain largely unexplored. Although mechanistic interpretability has successfully identified circuits in language and vision models, it has not yet been applied to SR. In this article, we introduce PATCHES, an evolutionary circuit discovery algorithm that identifies compact and correct circuits for SR. Using PATCHES, we isolate 28 circuits, providing the first circuit-level characterisation of an SR transformer. We validate these findings through a robust causal evaluation framework based on key notions such as faithfulness, completeness, and minimality. Our analysis shows that mean patching with performance-based evaluation most reliably isolates functionally correct circuits. In contrast, we demonstrate that direct logit attribution and probing classifiers primarily capture correlational features rather than causal ones, limiting their utility for circuit discovery. Overall, these results establish SR as a high-potential application domain for mechanistic interpretability and propose a principled methodology for circuit discovery.

papers.title: Crosscoding Through Time: Tracking Emergence & Consolidation Of Linguistic Representations Throughout LLM Pretraining
papers.research_question: How do linguistic features emerge and evolve during the pretraining of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a method using sparse crosscoders and the Relative Indirect Effect (RELIE) metric to track the emergence and evolution of linguistic features during LLM pretraining.
papers.conclusion: The approach is architecture-agnostic and scalable, offering a promising path toward more interpretable and fine-grained analysis of representation learning throughout pretraining.
papers.key_findings:
Crosscoders can detect feature emergence, maintenance, and discontinuation during pretraining.
Features evolve from token-specific detectors to abstract syntactic concepts over training time.
The Relative Indirect Effect (RELIE) metric effectively traces the causal importance of features across checkpoints.
The method is architecture-agnostic and scalable to billion-parameter models.
Multilingual models develop cross-lingual feature sharing, with abstract concepts becoming more universal over time.
papers.limitation: Early checkpoints may resist sparse mapping and accurate reconstruction with crosscoders.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) learn non-trivial abstractions during pretraining, like detecting irregular plural noun subjects. However, it is not well understood when and how specific linguistic abilities emerge as traditional evaluation methods such as benchmarking fail to reveal how models acquire concepts and capabilities. To bridge this gap and better understand model training at the concept level, we use sparse crosscoders to discover and align features across model checkpoints. Using this approach, we track the evolution of linguistic features during pretraining. We train crosscoders between open-sourced checkpoint triplets with significant performance and representation shifts, and introduce a novel metric, Relative Indirect Effects (RelIE), to trace training stages at which individual features become causally important for task performance. We show that crosscoders can detect feature emergence, maintenance, and discontinuation during pretraining. Our approach is architecture-agnostic and scalable, offering a promising path toward more interpretable and fine-grained analysis of representation learning throughout pretraining.

papers.title: How Does Controllability Emerge In Language Models During Pretraining?
papers.research_question: How does linear steerability emerge in language models during pretraining, and why does it vary across concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Linear steerability emerges during intermediate stages of training, varies across concepts, and is linked to increasing linear separability of concepts in the hidden space.
papers.conclusion: Linear steerability does not emerge uniformly but develops over training and varies between concepts, aligning with increasingly structured internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Linear steerability emerges in later training stages, separate from reasoning capability and emotion expression via prompting.
Emergence times vary widely across concepts, such as anger emerging earlier than sadness.
Concept representations become increasingly linearly separable in the hidden space as training progresses.
The Intervention Detector (ID) framework can reveal steerability dynamics and predict when linear steerability emerges.
These findings hold across different model families, indicating a general pattern.
papers.limitation:
Only evaluated on 7B-scale open-source models, not tested on larger LLMs.
Intervention coefficient was empirically tuned and differs across models, with underlying causes not investigated.
Did not explore alternative nonlinear approaches for extracting or intervening in model representations.
Methodological innovation in intervention techniques is not the focus; core procedure is consistent with prior work.
Alternative unsupervised methods such as mean-difference vectors are not compared.
Concepts like emotions lack ground truth, making evaluation subjective and based on semantic interpretation.
Steering certain concepts can produce offensive outputs, with no safety filtering applied.
future_direction: Examining how different pre-training corpora influence intervention outcomes.
Exploring alternative steering methods beyond PCA or K-Means.
Comparing unsupervised methods like mean-difference vectors and their influence on downstream intervention performance.
papers.abstract: Language models can be steered by modifying their internal representations to control concepts such as emotion, style, or truthfulness in generation. However, the conditions for an effective intervention remain unclear and are often validated through heuristics and trial-and-error. To fill this gap, we demonstrate that intervention efficacy, measured by linear steerability (i.e., the ability to adjust output via linear transformations of hidden states), emerges during intermediate stages of training. Moreover, even closely related concepts (e.g., anger and sadness) exhibit steerability emergence at distinct stages of training. To better interpret the dynamics of steerability during training, we adapt existing intervention techniques into a unified framework, referred to as the "Intervention Detector" (ID), which is designed to reveal how linear steerability evolves over the course of training through hidden state and representation analysis. ID reveals that concepts become increasingly linearly separable in the hidden space as training progresses, which strongly correlates with the emergence of linear steerability. We further introduce ID-based metrics, such as heatmaps, entropy trends, and cosine similarity, to help interpret how linear steerability evolves throughout training. In addition, we apply ID across different model families to ensure the generality of our findings on steerability dynamics.

papers.title: The Local Interaction Basis: Identifying Computationally-Relevant and Sparsely Interacting Features in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Can the Local Interaction Basis (LIB) method find interpretable and sparsely-interacting features in neural networks, particularly in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Local Interaction Basis (LIB), a method to transform neural network activations into a basis of computationally-relevant and sparsely-interacting features, and shows it works on toy models but not on language models.
papers.conclusion: LIB is promising on toy models but does not achieve interpretable and sparsely-interacting features on language models, likely due to the assumption of a linear non-overcomplete basis.
papers.key_findings:
LIB identifies more computationally-relevant features than PCA in modular addition and CIFAR-10 models.
LIB features interact more sparsely than PCA features in CIFAR-10 and some layers of language models.
LIB does not produce more interpretable features than PCA in language models.
Integrated gradient interaction graphs can aid circuit discovery in toy models.
LIB does not reveal modular structure in language models.
papers.limitation: LIB does not yield substantial improvements in interpretability or interaction sparsity when applied to language models.
future_direction: Generalizing LIB to overcomplete bases to handle features in superposition.
Exploring other ways to average attributions over the dataset.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the behavior of neural networks by reverse-engineering their internal computations. However, current methods struggle to find clear interpretations of neural network activations because a decomposition of activations into computational features is missing. Individual neurons or model components do not cleanly correspond to distinct features or functions. We present a novel interpretability method that aims to overcome this limitation by transforming the activations of the network into a new basis - the Local Interaction Basis (LIB). LIB aims to identify computational features by removing irrelevant activations and interactions. Our method drops irrelevant activation directions and aligns the basis with the singular vectors of the Jacobian matrix between adjacent layers. It also scales features based on their importance for downstream computation, producing an interaction graph that shows all computationally-relevant features and interactions in a model. We evaluate the effectiveness of LIB on modular addition and CIFAR-10 models, finding that it identifies more computationally-relevant features that interact more sparsely, compared to principal component analysis. However, LIB does not yield substantial improvements in interpretability or interaction sparsity when applied to language models. We conclude that LIB is a promising theory-driven approach for analyzing neural networks, but in its current form is not applicable to large language models.

papers.title: A Teacher-Student Perspective on the Dynamics of Learning Near the Optimal Point
papers.research_question: How does the evolution of the loss function for a student initialized near the optimal point depend on the characteristics (number of parameters, activation functions) of the network? Under which conditions can the Hessian rank at the optimal point be interpreted as an effective number of parameters?
papers.core_contribution: The paper characterizes the Hessian eigenspectrum in teacher-student setups and shows that the Hessian rank can serve as an effective parameter count for polynomial networks, but not for networks with non-polynomial activations like the error function.
papers.conclusion: The Hessian rank is a valid measure of effective parameters for polynomial networks with sufficiently large hidden layers, but for non-polynomial activations like the error function, the Hessian is full rank and no compression occurs.
papers.key_findings:
For linear networks, the Hessian eigenspectrum asymptotically follows a convolution of a scaled chi-squared distribution with a scaled Marchenko-Pastur distribution.
The long-time behavior of the loss function near the optimum is determined by the smallest non-zero eigenvalue of the Hessian.
For polynomial networks, the Hessian rank gives an effective number of parameters, with an upper bound derived for degree-n polynomials.
For the error function activation, the Hessian is always full rank, indicating no parameter compression is possible.
The number of effective parameters for a quadratic network is given by a specific formula that depends on input and hidden layer sizes.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to teacher-student setups with matching architectures and initialization near the optimal point.
future_direction: Study the effect of adding biases on the effective number of parameters.
Generalize the results to deeper networks.
Study the effects of over-parameterization on student networks and the Hessian rank evolution with time.
papers.abstract: Near an optimal learning point of a neural network, the learning performance of gradient descent dynamics is dictated by the Hessian matrix of the loss function with respect to the network parameters. We characterize the Hessian eigenspectrum for some classes of teacher-student problems, when the teacher and student networks have matching weights, showing that the smaller eigenvalues of the Hessian determine long-time learning performance. For linear networks, we analytically establish that for large networks the spectrum asymptotically follows a convolution of a scaled chi-square distribution with a scaled Marchenko-Pastur distribution. We numerically analyse the Hessian spectrum for polynomial and other non-linear networks. Furthermore, we show that the rank of the Hessian matrix can be seen as an effective number of parameters for networks using polynomial activation functions. For a generic non-linear activation function, such as the error function, we empirically observe that the Hessian matrix is always full rank.

papers.title: Memory Retrieval and Consolidation in Large Language Models through Function Tokens
papers.research_question: How is memory retrieved during inference and consolidated during pre-training in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Function Token Hypothesis to explain memory retrieval and consolidation in LLMs, where function tokens activate predictive features during inference and drive feature learning during pre-training.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes and provides evidence for the Function Token Hypothesis, which explains how function tokens drive memory retrieval and consolidation in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
During inference, a small set of function tokens activate the majority of the model's features.
Function tokens dynamically reactivate the most predictive features from the context to guide next-token prediction.
During pre-training, the prediction of content tokens following function tokens dominates the loss and drives feature expansion.
Pre-training initially focuses on learning to predict function tokens before learning content tokens.
Scaling model size primarily enhances the prediction of content tokens.
papers.limitation: The paper does not explain how function tokens acquire the ability to dynamically activate predictive features.
future_direction: How function tokens acquire the ability to dynamically activate predictive features.
How post-training modifies activation patterns in function tokens.
The dynamics of feature formation and the underlying reason for the scale-free property of token-feature activation.
papers.abstract: The remarkable success of large language models (LLMs) stems from their ability to consolidate vast amounts of knowledge into the memory during pre-training and to retrieve it from the memory during inference, enabling advanced capabilities such as knowledge memorization, instruction-following and reasoning. However, the mechanisms of memory retrieval and consolidation in LLMs remain poorly understood. In this paper, we propose the function token hypothesis to explain the workings of LLMs: During inference, function tokens activate the most predictive features from context and govern next token prediction (memory retrieval). During pre-training, predicting the next tokens (usually content tokens) that follow function tokens increases the number of learned features of LLMs and updates the model parameters (memory consolidation). Function tokens here roughly correspond to function words in linguistics, including punctuation marks, articles, prepositions, and conjunctions, in contrast to content tokens. We provide extensive experimental evidence supporting this hypothesis. Using bipartite graph analysis, we show that a small number of function tokens activate the majority of features. Case studies further reveal how function tokens activate the most predictive features from context to direct next token prediction. We also find that during pre-training, the training loss is dominated by predicting the next content tokens following function tokens, which forces the function tokens to select the most predictive features from context.

papers.title: The Mystery of In-Context Learning: A Comprehensive Survey on Interpretation and Analysis
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents a thorough survey on the interpretation and analysis of in-context learning (ICL) in large language models, organizing existing research into theoretical and empirical perspectives.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes by discussing open questions and challenges, and suggests potential avenues for future research, establishing the basis for further exploration into the interpretation of in-context learning.
papers.limitation: The survey is limited by space and primarily focuses on the ICL ability, excluding other emergent capabilities such as chain-of-thought and instruction following.
future_direction: Interpretation of ICL in Multimodal LLMs
Interpretation of ICL in Non-Transformer Architectures
Interpretation of ICL in Agentic Systems
papers.abstract: Understanding in-context learning (ICL) capability that enables large language models (LLMs) to excel in proficiency through demonstration examples is of utmost importance. This importance stems not only from the better utilization of this capability across various tasks, but also from the proactive identification and mitigation of potential risks, including concerns regarding truthfulness, bias, and toxicity, that may arise alongside the capability. In this paper, we present a thorough survey on the interpretation and analysis of in-context learning. First, we provide a concise introduction to the background and definition of in-context learning. Then, we give an overview of advancements from two perspectives: 1) a theoretical perspective, emphasizing studies on mechanistic interpretability and delving into the mathematical foundations behind ICL; and 2) an empirical perspective, concerning studies that empirically analyze factors associated with ICL. We conclude by highlighting the challenges encountered and suggesting potential avenues for future research. We believe that our work establishes the basis for further exploration into the interpretation of in-context learning. Additionally, we have created a repository containing the resources referenced in our survey.

papers.title: Schema-learning and rebinding as mechanisms of in-context learning and emergence
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning work, and can it be explained through schema-learning and rebinding mechanisms in interpretable models like clone-structured causal graphs (CSCGs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that in-context learning can be achieved through schema-learning and rebinding mechanisms in interpretable clone-structured causal graphs, providing insights into how ICL works in large language models.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that schema-learning and rebinding mechanisms in CSCGs can explain in-context learning, offering insights for designing interpretable architectures and understanding emergence in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
CSCG achieves in-context learning on the GINC dataset, accurately retrieving latent concepts.
CSCG learns template circuits for algorithms and generalizes to novel tokens through rebinding on the LIALT dataset.
ICL performance improves with model overparameterization, suggesting emergence is related to capacity.
CSCG can inductively learn new word usage from single examples in the dax test.
The mechanisms of schema-learning and rebinding in CSCGs provide a plausible explanation for ICL in transformers.
papers.limitation:
CSCG fails to generalize to concepts unseen during training, similar to transformers.
Imperfections in learned CSCG models can lead to failure cases, such as wrong schema retrieval.
future_direction: Designing novel architectures based on schema-learning and rebinding principles.
Searching for interpretable and editable circuits in transformers using the identified mechanisms.
Extending the approach to more complex tasks and datasets.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) is one of the most powerful and most unexpected capabilities to emerge in recent transformer-based large language models (LLMs). Yet the mechanisms that underlie it are poorly understood. In this paper, we demonstrate that comparable ICL capabilities can be acquired by an alternative sequence prediction learning method using clone-structured causal graphs (CSCGs). Moreover, a key property of CSCGs is that, unlike transformer-based LLMs, they are {\em interpretable}, which considerably simplifies the task of explaining how ICL works. Specifically, we show that it uses a combination of (a) learning template (schema) circuits for pattern completion, (b) retrieving relevant templates in a context-sensitive manner, and (c) rebinding of novel tokens to appropriate slots in the templates. We go on to marshall evidence for the hypothesis that similar mechanisms underlie ICL in LLMs. For example, we find that, with CSCGs as with LLMs, different capabilities emerge at different levels of overparameterization, suggesting that overparameterization helps in learning more complex template (schema) circuits. By showing how ICL can be achieved with small models and datasets, we open up a path to novel architectures, and take a vital step towards a more general understanding of the mechanics behind this important capability.

papers.title: Instruction-tuning Aligns LLMs to the Human Brain
papers.research_question: What is the effect of instruction-tuning on aligning LLM and human language processing mechanisms in terms of brain alignment and behavioral alignment?
papers.core_contribution: Instruction-tuning improves brain alignment between LLMs and the human brain, and this improvement is strongly correlated with the model's world knowledge representations.
papers.conclusion: Instruction-tuning aligns LLM representations to human brain activity, and this alignment is driven by improved world knowledge representations in the models.
papers.key_findings:
Instruction-tuning improves brain alignment by an average of 6.2% across tested LLMs.
Brain alignment is strongly correlated with model size (r=0.95) and world knowledge (r=0.81).
Instruction-tuning does not improve behavioral alignment to human reading times.
Brain alignment improvements are due to both additional training data and training to understand and follow instructions.
Smaller instruction-tuned models can achieve higher brain alignment than larger vanilla models.
papers.limitation: The BLANK2014 dataset has fewer participants (N=5) leading to greater noise in the results.
future_direction: Extend analysis to other modalities (e.g., vision, audio) and tasks (e.g., code generation, mathematical reasoning).
Study other model families and training methods.
Investigate the relationship between brain alignment and other model properties.
papers.abstract: Instruction-tuning is a widely adopted finetuning method that enables large language models (LLMs) to generate output that more closely resembles human responses. However, no studies have shown that instruction-tuning actually teaches LLMs to process language in a similar manner as humans. We investigate the effect of instruction-tuning on aligning LLM and human language processing mechanisms in two ways: (1) brain alignment, the similarity of LLM internal representations to neural activity in the human language system, and (2) behavioral alignment, the similarity of LLM and human behavior on a reading task. We assess 25 vanilla and instruction-tuned LLMs on three datasets involving humans reading naturalistic stories and sentences, and find that instruction-tuning generally enhances brain alignment (~6%), but has no similar effect on behavioral alignment. To identify factors underlying this improvement in brain alignment, we compute correlations between brain alignment and various LLM properties, such as model size, problem-solving, and world knowledge understanding. Notably, we find a strong positive correlation between brain alignment and model size (r = 0.95), as well as performance on tasks requiring world knowledge (r = 0.81). Our results demonstrate that instruction-tuning LLMs improves both world knowledge representations and brain alignment, suggesting that the mechanisms that encode world knowledge in LLMs also improve representational alignment to the human brain.

papers.title: Patterning: The Dual of Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the dual problem to interpretability? The paper introduces patterning as the dual: given a desired form of generalization, determine what training data leads to it.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces patterning as the dual of interpretability, using susceptibilities to derive data interventions that steer internal structure formation in neural networks, demonstrated in small language models and a synthetic task.
papers.conclusion: Patterning provides a principled approach to steering generalization by inverting the susceptibility relationship, with potential applications to AI alignment and control of internal structure.
papers.key_findings:
Re-weighting training data along the second principal susceptibility direction can accelerate or delay the formation of the induction circuit.
In the parentheses balancing task, patterning can select which algorithm the model learns by targeting the local learning coefficient of each solution.
Susceptibility-guided interventions produce predictable changes in internal structures.
papers.limitation:
Experiments use small models (3M parameters) and simple tasks.
Susceptibility estimation is computationally expensive.
Focus on one-off interventions made at the start of training, not online control.
Theoretical framework assumes infinitesimal perturbations, while practical interventions are finite; understanding when the linear approximation breaks down is important.
Connection between observables and downstream behavior (e.g., safety properties) requires further study.
future_direction: Develop online control (adjusting data distribution dynamically during training).
Scale to larger models and more efficient methods.
Study the connection to safety properties and AI alignment applications.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand how neural networks generalize beyond their training data by reverse-engineering their internal structures. We introduce patterning as the dual problem: given a desired form of generalization, determine what training data produces it. Our approach is based on susceptibilities, which measure how posterior expectation values of observables respond to infinitesimal shifts in the data distribution. Inverting this linear response relationship yields the data intervention that steers the model toward a target internal configuration. We demonstrate patterning in a small language model, showing that re-weighting training data along principal susceptibility directions can accelerate or delay the formation of structure, such as the induction circuit. In a synthetic parentheses balancing task where multiple algorithms achieve perfect training accuracy, we show that patterning can select which algorithm the model learns by targeting the local learning coefficient of each solution. These results establish that the same mathematical framework used to read internal structure can be inverted to write it.

papers.title: LLM world models are mental: Output layer evidence of brittle world model use in LLM mechanical reasoning
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) construct and manipulate internal 'world models,' or do they rely solely on statistical associations represented as output layer token probabilities learned from data?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs show some ability to reason about mechanical systems (pulley systems) using heuristics like pulley counting and can differentiate functional from jumbled systems, but their internal representations are brittle and fail when the task requires understanding of nuanced structural connectivity, indicating limited world model use.
papers.conclusion: The findings offer mixed support for the view that LLMs reason over world models independently from output token probabilities. The brittleness of these representations, especially in Study 3, aligns with critiques emphasizing the lack of robustness and generality in current systems.
papers.key_findings:
In Study 1, LLMs performed above chance in estimating mechanical advantage (MA) and their estimates correlated with ground truth MA, but they relied on a pulley-counting heuristic and selectively attended to relevant features.
LLMs could distinguish functional from non-functional (jumbled) pulley systems with high accuracy (F1=0.8) in Study 2.
In Study 3, LLMs failed to differentiate functional from non-functional (but connected) pulley systems, performing at chance level (F1=0.46).
The results suggest LLMs have some latent knowledge of pulley systems but lack robust internal models for nuanced structural reasoning.
The brittleness of these representations aligns with critiques emphasizing the lack of robustness and generality in current systems.
papers.limitation:
Uncertainty regarding whether tested pulley stimuli are truly out-of-distribution; exposure during training cannot be ruled out.
Difficulty deconfounding output layer token representations from potential latent world models represented in network weights without combining with interpretability research.
future_direction: Future work should further deconfound pulley count from MA and employ novel or synthetic diagramming languages to limit reliance on familiar formats like TikZ.
Extending the paradigm to other physical systems (e.g., levers, gear trains) may help assess the breadth of these internal representations.
Integrating the present approach with interpretability research may help elucidate the network circuits underlying reasoning over world models.
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) construct and manipulate internal world models, or do they rely solely on statistical associations represented as output layer token probabilities? We adapt cognitive science methodologies from human mental models research to test LLMs on pulley system problems using TikZ-rendered stimuli. Study 1 examines whether LLMs can estimate mechanical advantage (MA). State-of-the-art models performed marginally but significantly above chance, and their estimates correlated significantly with ground-truth MA. Significant correlations between number of pulleys and model estimates suggest that models employed a pulley counting heuristic, without necessarily simulating pulley systems to derive precise values. Study 2 tested this by probing whether LLMs represent global features crucial to MA estimation. Models evaluated a functionally connected pulley system against a fake system with randomly placed components. Without explicit cues, models identified the functional system as having greater MA with F1=0.8, suggesting LLMs could represent systems well enough to differentiate jumbled from functional systems. Study 3 built on this by asking LLMs to compare functional systems with matched systems which were connected up but which transferred no force to the weight; LLMs identified the functional system with F1=0.46, suggesting random guessing. Insofar as they may generalize, these findings are compatible with the notion that LLMs manipulate internal world models, sufficient to exploit statistical associations between pulley count and MA (Study 1), and to approximately represent system components' spatial relations (Study 2). However, they may lack the facility to reason over nuanced structural connectivity (Study 3). We conclude by advocating the utility of cognitive scientific methods to evaluate the world-modeling capacities of artificial intelligence systems.

papers.title: Subspace Chronicles: How Linguistic Information Emerges, Shifts and Interacts during Language Model Training
papers.research_question: How and when during language model training do different types of linguistic information (syntax, semantics, reasoning) emerge, shift, and interact?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an information-theoretic probing suite to extract and compare task-specific representational subspaces, revealing critical learning phases during LM training where linguistic information emerges, shares information, and later disentangles to specialize.
papers.conclusion: The subspace-based approach provides deeper insights into LM learning dynamics, showing that linguistic information continues to change even after performance stabilizes, and that cross-task similarities follow linguistic intuitions, with implications for interpretability, multi-task learning, and learning from limited data.
papers.key_findings:
Syntactic knowledge is acquired rapidly after 0.5% of full training.
Continued performance improvements primarily stem from acquisition of open-domain knowledge, while semantics and reasoning tasks benefit from later boosts to long-range contextualization and higher specialization.
Cross-task similarity reveals that linguistically related tasks share information throughout training, and do so more during the critical phase of learning than before or after.
Representational subspaces continue to shift even after performance plateaus, indicating ongoing refinement of linguistic information.
The layer depth at which task information is most salient (center of gravity) changes over time, with tasks specializing to different layers later in training.
papers.limitation:
Lack of compute and training statistics for gradient-level analysis.
Linear probes may not capture more complex information for tasks like QA and NLI.
The study is limited to BERT architecture and may not generalize to larger autoregressive LMs.
The study is correlatory and does not include targeted interventions.
future_direction: Verify whether the observed dynamics hold for larger, autoregressive LMs.
Investigate early-stage multi-task learning for better downstream performance.
Revisit training encoders for under-resourced languages given the early acquisition of linguistic information.
papers.abstract: Representational spaces learned via language modeling are fundamental to Natural Language Processing (NLP), however there has been limited understanding regarding how and when during training various types of linguistic information emerge and interact. Leveraging a novel information theoretic probing suite, which enables direct comparisons of not just task performance, but their representational subspaces, we analyze nine tasks covering syntax, semantics and reasoning, across 2M pre-training steps and five seeds. We identify critical learning phases across tasks and time, during which subspaces emerge, share information, and later disentangle to specialize. Across these phases, syntactic knowledge is acquired rapidly after 0.5% of full training. Continued performance improvements primarily stem from the acquisition of open-domain knowledge, while semantics and reasoning tasks benefit from later boosts to long-range contextualization and higher specialization. Measuring cross-task similarity further reveals that linguistically related tasks share information throughout training, and do so more during the critical phase of learning than before or after. Our findings have implications for model interpretability, multi-task learning, and learning from limited data.

papers.title: Differentiation and Specialization of Attention Heads via the Refined Local Learning Coefficient
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in a transformer language model differentiate and specialize during training, as revealed by refined local learning coefficients?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces refined local learning coefficients (rLLCs) as a principled, quantitative toolkit for developmental interpretability, revealing how attention heads differentiate and specialize during training and enabling the discovery of a novel multigram circuit.
papers.conclusion: Refined local learning coefficients provide a powerful toolkit for developmental interpretability, revealing the interplay between data distributional structure, loss landscape geometry, learning dynamics, and the resulting computational structure in neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Weight-refined LLCs (wrLLCs) reveal how attention heads differentiate into distinct functional types (e.g., induction heads, multigram heads) over the course of training.
Data-refined LLCs (drLLCs) show how heads specialize to different data distributions, such as one induction head specializing more to code.
The combination of refined LLCs leads to the identification of a novel multigram circuit involving coordination between layer 0 and layer 1 multigram heads.
The developmental perspective (evolution over time) is crucial for understanding the emergence of internal structure; point estimates at the end of training are insufficient.
