Leveraging a novel information theoretic probing suite, which enables direct comparisons of not just task performance, but their representational subspaces, we analyze nine tasks covering syntax, semantics and reasoning, across 2M pre-training steps and five seeds. We identify critical learning phases across tasks and time, during which subspaces emerge, share information, and later disentangle to specialize. Across these phases, syntactic knowledge is acquired rapidly after 0.5% of full training. Continued performance improvements primarily stem from the acquisition of open-domain knowledge, while semantics and reasoning tasks benefit from later boosts to long-range contextualization and higher specialization. Measuring cross-task similarity further reveals that linguistically related tasks share information throughout training, and do so more during the critical phase of learning than before or after. Our findings have implications for model interpretability, multi-task learning, and learning from limited data.

papers.title: Differentiation and Specialization of Attention Heads via the Refined Local Learning Coefficient
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in a transformer language model differentiate and specialize during training, as revealed by refined local learning coefficients?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces refined local learning coefficients (rLLCs) as a principled, quantitative toolkit for developmental interpretability, revealing how attention heads differentiate and specialize during training and enabling the discovery of a novel multigram circuit.
papers.conclusion: Refined local learning coefficients provide a powerful toolkit for developmental interpretability, revealing the interplay between data distributional structure, loss landscape geometry, learning dynamics, and the resulting computational structure in neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Weight-refined LLCs (wrLLCs) reveal how attention heads differentiate into distinct functional types (e.g., induction heads, multigram heads) over the course of training.
Data-refined LLCs (drLLCs) show how heads specialize to different data distributions, such as one induction head specializing more to code.
The combination of refined LLCs leads to the identification of a novel multigram circuit involving coordination between layer 0 and layer 1 multigram heads.
The developmental perspective (evolution over time) is crucial for understanding the emergence of internal structure; point estimates at the end of training are insufficient.
Refined LLCs provide a quantitative link between data distributional structure, geometric properties of the loss landscape, learning dynamics, and emergent computational structures.
papers.limitation:
The justification of the LLC estimator presumes that w* is a local minima of the population loss, but there is no clear way to ascertain this in practice, and estimates are often performed during training where this is unlikely.
The ground truth LLC is unknown, so the accuracy of estimated LLC values cannot be guaranteed, though there is reason to believe the ordinality is correct.
future_direction: Establishing the correspondence between data distributional structure, geometric properties of the loss landscape, learning dynamics, and emergent computational structures in neural networks.
papers.abstract: We introduce refined variants of the Local Learning Coefficient (LLC), a measure of model complexity grounded in singular learning theory, to study the development of internal structure in transformer language models during training. By applying these \textit{refined LLCs} (rLLCs) to individual components of a two-layer attention-only transformer, we gain novel insights into the progressive differentiation and specialization of attention heads. Our methodology reveals how attention heads differentiate into distinct functional roles over the course of training, analyzes the types of data these heads specialize to process, and discovers a previously unidentified multigram circuit. These findings demonstrate that rLLCs provide a principled, quantitative toolkit for \textit{developmental interpretability}, which aims to understand models through their evolution across the learning process. More broadly, this work takes a step towards establishing the correspondence between data distributional structure, geometric properties of the loss landscape, learning dynamics, and emergent computational structures in neural networks.

papers.title: Synergistic information supports modality integration and flexible learning in neural networks solving multiple tasks
papers.research_question: How and why synergistic information emerges in cognitive systems, and how these informational states map onto artificial neural networks in various learning modes.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that redundant information is required for robustness to perturbations, while synergistic information supports the integration of multiple modalities and enables flexible and efficient learning in neural networks.
papers.conclusion: Synergistic information is crucial for general-purpose learning as it supports integration of multiple modalities and flexible learning, while redundant information provides robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Synergy increases as neural networks learn multiple diverse tasks.
Performance in tasks requiring integration of multiple information sources critically relies on synergistic neurons.
Dropout increases network redundancy, corresponding to an increase in robustness.
Synergy is specifically linked to the integration of multiple modalities and flexible learning.
Redundant information provides robustness but is less efficient.
future_direction: Future work may seek to disentangle the relevance of each potential cause driving the importance of synergistic neurons.
Empirical evaluation of the conjectures about unique information in specialized circuits is an interesting avenue.
papers.abstract: Striking progress has recently been made in understanding human cognition by analyzing how its neuronal underpinnings are engaged in different modes of information processing. Specifically, neural information can be decomposed into synergistic, redundant, and unique features, with synergistic components being particularly aligned with complex cognition. However, two fundamental questions remain unanswered: (a) precisely how and why a cognitive system can become highly synergistic; and (b) how these informational states map onto artificial neural networks in various learning modes. To address these questions, here we employ an information-decomposition framework to investigate the information processing strategies adopted by simple artificial neural networks performing a variety of cognitive tasks in both supervised and reinforcement learning settings. Our results show that synergy increases as neural networks learn multiple diverse tasks. Furthermore, performance in tasks requiring integration of multiple information sources critically relies on synergistic neurons. Finally, randomly turning off neurons during training through dropout increases network redundancy, corresponding to an increase in robustness. Overall, our results suggest that while redundant information is required for robustness to perturbations in the learning process, synergistic information is used to combine information from multiple modalities -- and more generally for flexible and efficient learning. These findings open the door to new ways of investigating how and why learning systems employ specific information-processing strategies, and support the principle that the capacity for general-purpose learning critically relies in the system's information dynamics.

papers.title: Exploring Concept Depth: How Large Language Models Acquire Knowledge and Concept at Different Layers?
papers.research_question: Can shallow layers in LLMs capture meaningful features of simple knowledge, while complex concepts need deeper layers to capture their meaningful features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of 'Concept Depth' to measure how different layers in LLMs capture concepts of varying complexity, showing that simpler concepts are learned in shallow layers while complex concepts require deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: The Concept Depth metric provides a useful framework for understanding how LLMs process concepts of varying complexity across layers, and the experimental insights enhance the understanding of internal representations in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler concepts (e.g., factual knowledge) are learned in shallow layers, while more complex concepts (e.g., reasoning tasks) require deeper layers for accurate understanding.
The pattern of Concept Depth is consistent across different model families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) and model sizes.
Larger models within a family tend to achieve higher peak accuracy and sometimes converge to optimal performance at earlier layers.
Adding noise to the input or quantizing model weights (e.g., to 8-bit) slows down the convergence of concept understanding, requiring deeper layers to achieve comparable accuracy.
Compressing models to 16-bit quantization does not significantly harm the understanding process compared to 32-bit.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performances across a wide range of tasks. However, the mechanisms by which these models encode tasks of varying complexities remain poorly understood. In this paper, we explore the hypothesis that LLMs process concepts of varying complexities in different layers, introducing the idea of "Concept Depth" to suggest that more complex concepts are typically acquired in deeper layers. Specifically, we categorize concepts based on their level of abstraction, defining them in the order of increasing complexity within factual, emotional, and inferential tasks. We conduct extensive probing experiments using layer-wise representations across various LLM families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) on various datasets spanning the three domains of tasks. Our findings reveal that models could efficiently conduct probing for simpler tasks in shallow layers, and more complex tasks typically necessitate deeper layers for accurate understanding. Additionally, we examine how external factors, such as adding noise to the input and quantizing the model weights, might affect layer-wise representations. Our findings suggest that these factors can impede the development of a conceptual understanding of LLMs until deeper layers are explored. We hope that our proposed concept and experimental insights will enhance the understanding of the mechanisms underlying LLMs. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Luckfort/CD.

papers.title: CLUE: Conflict-guided Localization for LLM Unlearning Framework
papers.research_question: How can we improve LLM unlearning by precisely localizing neurons responsible for forgetting and retaining, using circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CLUE, a framework that uses circuit discovery and CNF satisfiability to localize forget, retain, and conflict neurons for targeted unlearning, improving forget efficacy and retain utility.
papers.conclusion: CLUE offers more precise neuron localization and significantly outperforms existing methods in both forget efficacy and retain utility.
papers.key_findings:
CLUE outperforms existing localization methods in forget efficacy and retain utility with fewer modified parameters.
It successfully identifies forget, retain, and conflict neurons through CNF satisfiability of circuits.
The proportion of forget neurons increases and conflict neurons decreases after unlearning, indicating effective decoupling.
Circuit sparsity and faithfulness are correlated with unlearning efficacy.
CLUE provides more comprehensive interpretability by revealing neuron categories and their distributions.
papers.limitation:
The circuit is static and cannot dynamically reflect changes in key neurons during the fine-tuning process.
For multiple retain sets, the fine-tuning stage cannot provide targeted solutions for every possible conflict combination.
future_direction: Exploring the dynamics of circuits during parameter fine-tuning.
Developing editing methods other than fine-tuning for multiple retain sets.
papers.abstract: The LLM unlearning aims to eliminate the influence of undesirable data without affecting causally unrelated information. This process typically involves using a forget set to remove target information, alongside a retain set to maintain non-target capabilities. While recent localization-based methods demonstrate promise in identifying important neurons to be unlearned, they fail to disentangle neurons responsible for forgetting undesirable knowledge or retaining essential skills, often treating them as a single entangled group. As a result, these methods apply uniform interventions, risking catastrophic over-forgetting or incomplete erasure of the target knowledge. To address this, we turn to circuit discovery, a mechanistic interpretability technique, and propose the Conflict-guided Localization for LLM Unlearning framEwork (CLUE). This framework identifies the forget and retain circuit composed of important neurons, and then the circuits are transformed into conjunctive normal forms (CNF). The assignment of each neuron in the CNF satisfiability solution reveals whether it should be forgotten or retained. We then provide targeted fine-tuning strategies for different categories of neurons. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, compared to existing localization methods, CLUE achieves superior forget efficacy and retain utility through precise neural localization.

papers.title: Dissecting Lottery Ticket Transformers: Structural and Behavioral Study of Sparse Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How does iterative magnitude pruning affect the learned representations and internal structures of Transformers for neural machine translation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that iterative magnitude pruning degrades complex semantic knowledge first, causes higher layers to diverge and become less complex, shifts encoding burden to early layers, but leaves attention mechanisms largely unchanged.
papers.conclusion: The paper evaluates how unstructured pruning affects Transformer behavior while maintaining task performance, showing pruning degrades semantic knowledge before BLEU, early sparse layers better encode low-level information, representational changes occur in higher layers, and attention distributions remain similar.
papers.key_findings:
Complex semantic information is lost first during pruning, before BLEU decreases.
Model activations steadily diverge from unpruned representations, particularly at higher layers.
Information flow becomes more distributed in sparse Transformers: lower layers perform more encoding.
Attention mechanisms remain remarkably consistent across sparsities.
Encoder-decoder attention is the richest in representation, whereas decoder self-attention is the simplest.
papers.limitation:
BLEU is an imperfect measure of translation quality, so pruned models may perform worse than suggested.
The work focuses solely on magnitude pruning, which may not be representative of other pruning methods.
Probing classifiers measure correlation between model outputs and auxiliary information, not necessarily what information the model uses during its forward pass.
future_direction: Future work could analyze a model's encoded knowledge in other ways beyond probing.
Differences in how directly sparse and dense models encode information is an interesting question for future study, potentially using minimum description lengths.
papers.abstract: Recent work on the lottery ticket hypothesis has produced highly sparse Transformers for NMT while maintaining BLEU. However, it is unclear how such pruning techniques affect a model's learned representations. By probing Transformers with more and more lowmagnitude weights pruned away, we find that complex semantic information is first to be degraded. Analysis of internal activations reveals that higher layers diverge most over the course of pruning, gradually becoming less complex than their dense counterparts. Meanwhile, early layers of sparse models begin to perform more encoding. Attention mechanisms remain remarkably consistent as sparsity increases.

papers.title: Are formal and functional linguistic mechanisms dissociated in language models?
papers.research_question: Do current large language models exhibit distinct localization (dissociation) of formal and functional linguistic mechanisms in their internal circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds evidence for formal-functional dissociation in LLMs in terms of cross-task faithfulness (formal task circuits perform other formal tasks better than functional ones, and vice-versa), but not in terms of circuit overlap, suggesting a shared pool of mechanisms for formal tasks rather than a single unified region.
papers.conclusion: There is evidence for emerging formal-functional dissociation in LLMs in terms of cross-task faithfulness, but not in terms of circuit overlap, indicating a set of shared formal linguistic mechanisms rather than a single unified region.
papers.key_findings:
Circuits for formal and functional linguistic tasks have low overlap (IoU).
Circuits for formal tasks do not have especially high overlap with each other, arguing against a single unified formal network.
Formal task circuits perform other formal tasks better than they perform functional tasks (cross-task faithfulness).
Functional task circuits perform other functional tasks better than they perform formal tasks (cross-task faithfulness).
Clustering based on cross-task faithfulness vectors separates formal and functional tasks into distinct groups.
papers.limitation: The circuit-finding method (EAP-IG) may not perfectly capture all relevant mechanisms, and the findings are limited to the specific models and tasks studied.
future_direction: Studying more models and tasks to generalize findings.
Using more granular analyses (e.g., neuron-level, sparse feature circuits).
Investigating the effects of model scale and architecture on dissociation.
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable, these capabilities are unevenly distributed: they excel at formal linguistic tasks, such as producing fluent, grammatical text, but struggle more with functional linguistic tasks like reasoning and consistent fact retrieval. Inspired by neuroscience, recent work suggests that to succeed on both formal and functional linguistic tasks, LLMs should use different mechanisms for each; such localization could either be built-in or emerge spontaneously through training. In this paper, we ask: do current models, with fast-improving functional linguistic abilities, exhibit distinct localization of formal and functional linguistic mechanisms? We answer this by finding and comparing the "circuits", or minimal computational subgraphs, responsible for various formal and functional tasks. Comparing 5 LLMs across 10 distinct tasks, we find that while there is indeed little overlap between circuits for formal and functional tasks, there is also little overlap between formal linguistic tasks, as exists in the human brain. Thus, a single formal linguistic network, unified and distinct from functional task circuits, remains elusive. However, in terms of cross-task faithfulness - the ability of one circuit to solve another's task - we observe a separation between formal and functional mechanisms, suggesting that shared mechanisms between formal tasks may exist.

papers.title: Toward Mechanistic Explanation of Deductive Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does a small language model solve a deductive reasoning task, and what internal mechanisms (e.g., induction heads) are involved in implementing the logical inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a small language model can learn deductive reasoning by implementing rule-based circuits, with induction heads playing a central role, and introduces a truncated pseudoinverse technique for decoding query, key, and value information.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that a tiny LM can learn deductive reasoning by implementing symbolic rule-based circuits, with induction heads being a fundamental component, and suggests that induction heads may also be central in more complex logical reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
A simplified NanoGPT model trained with Chain-of-Thought can learn deductive reasoning rules and generalize to unseen examples.
Induction heads are crucial for implementing rule completion and rule chaining steps in the logical inference.
The model learns the underlying inference rules rather than memorizing patterns.
A single attention head can host multiple induction heads and other circuits, simplifying post-hoc explanation.
Training without Chain-of-Thought leads to memorization and poor generalization, indicating the importance of CoT for learning rules.
papers.limitation:
The interpretability techniques used (e.g., residual stream decoding and truncated pseudoinverse) are not 100% precise and may fail to decode the expected tokens.
The deductive reasoning task is simple and does not reflect the complexity of real-world logical reasoning.
future_direction: Investigating whether one-layer circuits resembling induction heads can be created by modifying the attention mechanism to decouple key and value positions.
Exploring the role of induction heads in solving more complex logical problems with larger language models.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have demonstrated relevant capabilities in solving problems that require logical reasoning; however, the corresponding internal mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we show that a small language model can solve a deductive reasoning task by learning the underlying rules (rather than operating as a statistical learner). A low-level explanation of its internal representations and computational circuits is then provided. Our findings reveal that induction heads play a central role in the implementation of the rule completion and rule chaining steps involved in the logical inference required by the task.

papers.title: DORA: Exploring Outlier Representations in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we analyze the representational space of deep neural networks to identify outlier representations that may correspond to spurious correlations or undesired concepts in a data-agnostic manner?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DORA, a data-agnostic framework for analyzing neural representations using a novel Extreme-Activation distance metric, which can identify outlier representations that often correspond to spurious or undesired concepts.
papers.conclusion: DORA offers an effective data-agnostic approach to explore and interpret neural representations, enabling the identification of anomalous representations that often encode spurious or undesired concepts, thereby enhancing model transparency and safety.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed Extreme-Activation distance metric aligns well with human judgment of concept similarity and outperforms traditional distance metrics in capturing semantic relationships.
DORA can effectively identify outlier representations that detect spurious correlations, such as watermarks or artifacts, in pre-trained models.
The framework is applicable across various architectures (CNNs, Transformers) and datasets (ImageNet, CIFAR-100).
Outlier representations corresponding to undesired concepts can persist even after fine-tuning on a different dataset.
DORA provides a practical tool for model interpretability and safety by revealing learned concepts that may lead to biased or harmful decisions.
papers.abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) excel at learning complex abstractions within their internal representations. However, the concepts they learn remain opaque, a problem that becomes particularly acute when models unintentionally learn spurious correlations. In this work, we present DORA (Data-agnOstic Representation Analysis), the first data-agnostic framework for analyzing the representational space of DNNs. Central to our framework is the proposed Extreme-Activation (EA) distance measure, which assesses similarities between representations by analyzing their activation patterns on data points that cause the highest level of activation. As spurious correlations often manifest in features of data that are anomalous to the desired task, such as watermarks or artifacts, we demonstrate that internal representations capable of detecting such artifactual concepts can be found by analyzing relationships within neural representations. We validate the EA metric quantitatively, demonstrating its effectiveness both in controlled scenarios and real-world applications. Finally, we provide practical examples from popular Computer Vision models to illustrate that representations identified as outliers using the EA metric often correspond to undesired and spurious concepts.

papers.title: Adaptive Circuit Behavior and Generalization in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How well does the indirect object identification (IOI) circuit in GPT-2 small generalize to prompt variants that challenge the assumptions of its algorithm?
papers.core_contribution: The IOI circuit generalizes surprisingly well to prompt variants, reusing all its components and mechanisms while only adding additional input edges, and a mechanism called S2 Hacking explains how the circuit outperforms the full model on these variants.
papers.conclusion: The IOI circuit in GPT-2 small generalizes more effectively than previously understood, reusing its core components and mechanisms while adapting through minimal structural changes, offering insights into the broader capabilities of large neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
The base IOI circuit outperforms the full model on DoubleIO and TripleIO prompt variants where the IOI algorithm would fail.
A mechanism termed S2 Hacking explains how the circuit achieves high performance on these variants by focusing on the S2 token due to the knockout procedure.
New circuits discovered for DoubleIO and TripleIO variants reuse all components of the base IOI circuit, only adding edges from additional input tokens (IO2 for DoubleIO, IO2 and IO3 for TripleIO).
The circuit components (attention heads) largely retain their functionalities from the base IOI task when evaluated on the variants.
The order of names in the prompt affects performance, with a 'first come, first serve' mechanism observed in a Previous Token head (2.2).
future_direction: a more detailed study of the duplicate suppression mechanism
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the inner workings of large neural networks by identifying circuits, or minimal subgraphs within the model that implement algorithms responsible for performing specific tasks. These circuits are typically discovered and analyzed using a narrowly defined prompt format. However, given the abilities of large language models (LLMs) to generalize across various prompt formats for the same task, it remains unclear how well these circuits generalize. For instance, it is unclear whether the models generalization results from reusing the same circuit components, the components behaving differently, or the use of entirely different components. In this paper, we investigate the generality of the indirect object identification (IOI) circuit in GPT-2 small, which is well-studied and believed to implement a simple, interpretable algorithm. We evaluate its performance on prompt variants that challenge the assumptions of this algorithm. Our findings reveal that the circuit generalizes surprisingly well, reusing all of its components and mechanisms while only adding additional input edges. Notably, the circuit generalizes even to prompt variants where the original algorithm should fail; we discover a mechanism that explains this which we term S2 Hacking. Our findings indicate that circuits within LLMs may be more flexible and general than previously recognized, underscoring the importance of studying circuit generalization to better understand the broader capabilities of these models.

papers.title: Unveiling In-Context Learning: A Coordinate System to Understand Its Working Mechanism
papers.research_question: What is the underlying working mechanism of in-context learning (ICL) in large language models, and how can conflicting views about the importance of similar examples versus task recognition be unified?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a two-dimensional coordinate system that unifies two conflicting views on in-context learning (ICL) by explaining ICL behavior through two orthogonal variables: task recognition (cognition) and the presence of similar examples (perception).
papers.conclusion: The proposed two-dimensional coordinate system provides a principled and universal framework for understanding the working mechanism of in-context learning across both classification and generation tasks.
papers.key_findings:
In the first quadrant (task recognized, similar examples present), models leverage both pre-trained knowledge and similar examples; incorrect labels in similar examples cause confusion, with smaller models more likely to copy incorrect labels.
In the second quadrant (task recognized, no similar examples), models rely primarily on pre-trained knowledge, and increasing the number of demonstration shots does not significantly improve performance.
In the third quadrant (task not recognized, no similar examples), ICL fails and models exhibit a strong positional bias, often predicting the label of the first example.
In the fourth quadrant (task not recognized, similar examples present), models directly copy the labels of similar examples, with performance heavily dependent on label correctness and larger models being better at recognizing similarity.
The proposed peak inverse rank (PIR) metric effectively quantifies a model's task recognition ability during ICL.
papers.limitation:
The coordinate system and analysis are primarily based on classification tasks, with generation tasks only briefly explored in a case study.
The study uses models up to 40B parameters; investigating larger models might reveal additional insights.
future_direction: Extend the coordinate system analysis to larger language models.
Apply the coordinate system to a broader range of tasks, especially generation tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable in-context learning (ICL) capabilities. However, the underlying working mechanism of ICL remains poorly understood. Recent research presents two conflicting views on ICL: One emphasizes the impact of similar examples in the demonstrations, stressing the need for label correctness and more shots. The other attributes it to LLMs' inherent ability of task recognition, deeming label correctness and shot numbers of demonstrations as not crucial. In this work, we provide a Two-Dimensional Coordinate System that unifies both views into a systematic framework. The framework explains the behavior of ICL through two orthogonal variables: whether similar examples are presented in the demonstrations (perception) and whether LLMs can recognize the task (cognition). We propose the peak inverse rank metric to detect the task recognition ability of LLMs and study LLMs' reactions to different definitions of similarity. Based on these, we conduct extensive experiments to elucidate how ICL functions across each quadrant on multiple representative classification tasks. Finally, we extend our analyses to generation tasks, showing that our coordinate system can also be used to interpret ICL for generation tasks effectively.

papers.title: Representational Distance Learning for Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can a student deep neural network learn from the internal representational spaces of a teacher model by matching their representational distance matrices (RDMs)?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Representational Distance Learning (RDL), a stochastic gradient descent method that uses auxiliary error functions to pull a student network's representational distance matrices (RDMs) toward those of a teacher network, enabling transfer learning even with architectural differences.
papers.conclusion: RDL is a promising method for transferring knowledge from a teacher model to a student DNN by matching their internal representational spaces, and may be used in the future to train DNNs using brain-activity measurements (e.g., fMRI-based RDMs) to build more realistic models of biological brains.
papers.key_findings:
RDL significantly improved visual classification performance on MNIST and CIFAR-100 compared to baseline networks without transfer learning.
RDL was competitive with other transfer learning techniques (finetuning, deep supervision, hints) on MNIST.
On CIFAR-100, RDL outperformed finetuning and performed comparably to deep supervision and hints.
Multidimensional scaling (MDS) visualizations showed that RDL pulled the student's RDMs toward the teacher's RDMs, especially at deeper layers.
RDL allows a student network to learn similar sequential transformations to those learned by a teacher network.
future_direction: Train DNNs using fMRI-based RDMs from the human visual ventral stream to build more realistic models of biological brains.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) provide useful models of visual representational transformations. We present a method that enables a DNN (student) to learn from the internal representational spaces of a reference model (teacher), which could be another DNN or, in the future, a biological brain. Representational spaces of the student and the teacher are characterized by representational distance matrices (RDMs). We propose representational distance learning (RDL), a stochastic gradient descent method that drives the RDMs of the student to approximate the RDMs of the teacher. We demonstrate that RDL is competitive with other transfer learning techniques for two publicly available benchmark computer vision datasets (MNIST and CIFAR-100), while allowing for architectural differences between student and teacher. By pulling the student's RDMs toward those of the teacher, RDL significantly improved visual classification performance when compared to baseline networks that did not use transfer learning. In the future, RDL may enable combined supervised training of deep neural networks using task constraints (e.g., images and category labels) and constraints from brain-activity measurements, so as to build models that replicate the internal representational spaces of biological brains.

papers.title: From Next-Token to Mathematics: The Learning Dynamics of Mathematical Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does mathematical reasoning ability develop during pre-training and post-training in LLMs, and how aligned are the learning trajectories with human curricula?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MathCAMPS, a fine-grained dataset for mathematical reasoning, and uses it to analyze learning dynamics, showing that mathematical skills are learned in an order correlated with human curriculum and that instruction tuning has varied effects on different skills.
papers.conclusion: MathCAMPS enables fine-grained analysis of mathematical reasoning, revealing insights into learning dynamics and the effects of instruction tuning, paving the way for an empirical understanding of LLM training dynamics in relation to reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Mathematical skills are learned during pre-training in an order that measurably correlates with the human-designed curriculum, even though training data are randomly ordered.
Skills evolve smoothly during training rather than emerging discretely at specific points.
Instruction tuning has varied effects: it improves some mathematical skills but degrades others, and the impact depends on the specific tuning methodology.
Models struggle more with fraction operations than with decimal operations, likely due to tokenization differences and the multi-step reasoning required for fractions.
Models are not robust to follow-up questions, showing significant accuracy drops when probed with incremental or counterfactual questions.
papers.limitation: The evaluation only covers computational problems and does not capture conceptual mathematical skills that human students also learn.
future_direction: Using MathCAMPS to inform model pre-training and evaluation for educational applications.
Using follow-up problems in MathCAMPS as a rich source for further analysis of model robustness and dialogue understanding.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) solely trained on next-token prediction learn to solve a wide range of problems involving mathematical reasoning. But how does this ability evolve during training? We show the first analysis of how mathematical reasoning abilities of several open-weight LLMs develop during pre-training and post-training. To this end, we construct MathCAMPS, a synthetic dataset of novel mathematical reasoning problems grounded in 44 fine-grained skills taken from the Common Core curriculum from K to 8th grades. In one experiment, we show that mathematical skills are learned during pre-training in an order that measurably correlates with the human-designed curriculum, even though training data are randomly ordered. We also show a detailed analysis of which mathematical abilities benefit from instruction tuning, a widely used post-training method and, in contrast, which skills suffer. Our work paves the way for an empirical understanding of LLM training dynamics in relation to reasoning.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Learning Representations: To What Extent Do Different Neural Networks Learn the Same Representation
papers.research_question: How similar are the representations learned by two networks with identical architecture but trained from different initializations?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a theory and algorithms based on neuron activation subspace match to analyze representation similarity in neural networks, and finds that representations learned by convolutional layers are not as similar as expected.
papers.conclusion: Representations learned by convolutional layers are not as similar as prevalently expected, raising fundamental questions about learning representations and interpretability in deep learning.
papers.key_findings:
Maximum match similarity is low for most convolutional layers, indicating low overall similarity of representations.
Layers close to input and output show higher similarity due to alignment with input data and output targets, respectively.
Simple matches are rarely of small size, indicating that single neurons or small neuron clusters do not learn similar representations.
The structure of matches can be characterized by maximum matches and simple matches, which can be found efficiently with the proposed algorithms.
The findings raise questions about whether networks learn completely different representations or if subspace match is not the right metric for similarity.
papers.limitation: Subspace match may not be the right metric for measuring the similarity of representations.
papers.abstract: It is widely believed that learning good representations is one of the main reasons for the success of deep neural networks. Although highly intuitive, there is a lack of theory and systematic approach quantitatively characterizing what representations do deep neural networks learn. In this work, we move a tiny step towards a theory and better understanding of the representations. Specifically, we study a simpler problem: How similar are the representations learned by two networks with identical architecture but trained from different initializations. We develop a rigorous theory based on the neuron activation subspace match model. The theory gives a complete characterization of the structure of neuron activation subspace matches, where the core concepts are maximum match and simple match which describe the overall and the finest similarity between sets of neurons in two networks respectively. We also propose efficient algorithms to find the maximum match and simple matches. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments using our algorithms. Experimental results suggest that, surprisingly, representations learned by the same convolutional layers of networks trained from different initializations are not as similar as prevalently expected, at least in terms of subspace match.

papers.title: Neural Network Memorization Dissection
papers.research_question: What is the difference between DNNs trained with random labels and the ones trained with true labels? How do DNNs prioritize the learning of simple patterns?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a dissection approach to measure similarity between what different DNNs have learned and memorized, and finds that DNNs have one consistent way to learn simple patterns but multiple ways to memorize random labels.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that DNNs learn simple patterns consistently but memorize random data in varied ways, establishing a connection between learning process and pattern complexity through gradient analysis.
papers.key_findings:
DNNs prioritize learning of simple patterns first, as indicated by gradient magnitude analysis during training.
The proposed dissection approach using Activation Maximization with GAN regularization can effectively measure similarity between learned functions of different DNNs.
DNNs trained on data with true labels learn similar functions regardless of random initialization, network size, or architecture (one way to learn).
DNNs trained on data with random labels memorize training samples in different ways each time (N ways to memorize).
With mixed noise levels in training data, DNNs learn simple patterns and memorize the rest, with similarity between models decreasing as noise increases.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) can easily fit a random labeling of the training data with zero training error. What is the difference between DNNs trained with random labels and the ones trained with true labels? Our paper answers this question with two contributions. First, we study the memorization properties of DNNs. Our empirical experiments shed light on how DNNs prioritize the learning of simple input patterns. In the second part, we propose to measure the similarity between what different DNNs have learned and memorized. With the proposed approach, we analyze and compare DNNs trained on data with true labels and random labels. The analysis shows that DNNs have \textit{One way to Learn} and \textit{N ways to Memorize}. We also use gradient information to gain an understanding of the analysis results.

papers.title: The Grammar-Learning Trajectories of Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: Do neural language models acquire linguistic phenomena in a consistent order during training, and what do their learning trajectories reveal about inductive biases?
papers.core_contribution: Neural language models acquire grammatical phenomena in a consistent order across different initializations, architectures, and training data, suggesting a shared inductive bias, and their learning trajectory is approximately one-dimensional.
papers.conclusion: NLMs exhibit consistent learning trajectories, providing a valuable perspective for studying their inductive biases and linguistic representations, complementary to analyzing final model states.
papers.key_findings:
NLMs with different random initializations learn grammatical phenomena in a highly correlated order.
Different architectures (GPT2, TransformerXL) show similar learning trajectories when aligned by overall performance.
The choice of training data affects the learning trajectory but does not override the shared order; correlation increases with training.
The learning trajectory is essentially one-dimensional: models with similar overall performance have similar grammatical knowledge.
Early learning stages rely on local cues (e.g., bag-of-words), while later stages incorporate more context and structural information.
future_direction: Investigate the impact of additional factors, architectures, and learning phases that appear later in training.
papers.abstract: The learning trajectories of linguistic phenomena in humans provide insight into linguistic representation, beyond what can be gleaned from inspecting the behavior of an adult speaker. To apply a similar approach to analyze neural language models (NLM), it is first necessary to establish that different models are similar enough in the generalizations they make. In this paper, we show that NLMs with different initialization, architecture, and training data acquire linguistic phenomena in a similar order, despite their different end performance. These findings suggest that there is some mutual inductive bias that underlies these models' learning of linguistic phenomena. Taking inspiration from psycholinguistics, we argue that studying this inductive bias is an opportunity to study the linguistic representation implicit in NLMs. Leveraging these findings, we compare the relative performance on different phenomena at varying learning stages with simpler reference models. Results suggest that NLMs exhibit consistent "developmental" stages. Moreover, we find the learning trajectory to be approximately one-dimensional: given an NLM with a certain overall performance, it is possible to predict what linguistic generalizations it has already acquired. Initial analysis of these stages presents phenomena clusters (notably morphological ones), whose performance progresses in unison, suggesting a potential link between the generalizations behind them.

papers.title: Self-Ablating Transformers: More Interpretability, Less Sparsity
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between sparsity and interpretability in transformers? Does inducing sparsity during training via a self-ablation mechanism enhance interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a self-ablation mechanism that enforces selective activation (k-winner-takes-all) during training, leading to improved interpretability (more localized circuits, specialized neurons) without necessarily increasing overall sparsity.
papers.conclusion: Self-ablation improves transformer interpretability across multiple indicators (circuit localization, feature disentanglement, neuron explainability) by promoting functional specialization and localized computation, challenging the simple intuition that sparsity alone leads to interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Self-ablation reduces circuit complexity, as shown by fewer edges in ACDC circuits for the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task.
Self-ablation leads to sparser feature representations (lower L0 norm in Sparse Autoencoders) and better reconstruction fidelity (higher CE score).
Self-ablation improves neuron explainability, with ablated models achieving higher automated explanation scores.
Self-ablation results in more focused neuron activation patterns, evidenced by lower graph density, lower transitivity, and increased specialization metrics in Neuron-to-Graph analysis.
Self-ablation incurs only a modest increase in validation perplexity, indicating a manageable trade-off between interpretability and language modeling performance.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation was conducted on the linguistically simple TinyStories dataset, which lacks complex syntax, diverse vocabulary, and abstract reasoning, limiting generalizability to real-world language.
Experiments were conducted on relatively small models; it is unknown how the self-ablation mechanism scales to much larger architectures.
future_direction: Evaluating self-ablation on linguistically diverse datasets to test scalability to complex linguistic phenomena.
Investigating the impact of model scale on the self-ablation mechanism's effects.
Exploring the application of self-ablation within a fine-tuning paradigm to improve interpretability of existing large language models.
papers.abstract: A growing intuition in machine learning suggests a link between sparsity and interpretability. We introduce a novel self-ablation mechanism to investigate this connection ante-hoc in the context of language transformers. Our approach dynamically enforces a k-winner-takes-all constraint, forcing the model to demonstrate selective activation across neuron and attention units. Unlike post-hoc methods that analyze already-trained models, our approach integrates interpretability directly into model training, promoting feature localization from inception. Training small models on the TinyStories dataset and employing interpretability tests, we find that self-ablation leads to more localized circuits, concentrated feature representations, and increased neuron specialization without compromising language modelling performance. Surprisingly, our method also decreased overall sparsity, indicating that self-ablation promotes specialization rather than widespread inactivity. This reveals a complex interplay between sparsity and interpretability, where decreased global sparsity can coexist with increased local specialization, leading to enhanced interpretability. To facilitate reproducibility, we make our code available at https://github.com/keenanpepper/self-ablating-transformers.

papers.title: APP: Accelerated Path Patching with Task-Specific Pruning
papers.research_question: Can pruning be used for circuit discovery, and how can we accelerate path patching by reducing the search space?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Accelerated Path Patching (APP), a hybrid method that uses Contrastive-FLAP pruning to reduce the search space for circuit discovery, achieving significant speedups while recovering minimal circuits with performance comparable to standard path patching.
papers.conclusion: APP provides a scalable preprocessing step for circuit discovery, making mechanistic interpretability more efficient and practical for large models.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning alone cannot recover minimal circuits; circuits found by pruning are larger than those found by path patching.
Contrastive-FLAP, a novel pruning method, better preserves task-specific attention heads compared to vanilla FLAP.
APP reduces the search space for circuit discovery by an average of 56%, leading to speedups of 59.63%-93.27% compared to standard path patching.
Circuits discovered by APP have substantial overlap and similar performance to those found by standard path patching.
APP enables circuit discovery to scale to larger models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B) by reducing computational costs.
papers.limitation:
Hyperparameter search is limited by computational cost, especially for large models.
Trade-off between circuit size and performance requires researcher discretion.
APP focuses on attention heads and does not include MLP components, which may be important for some tasks.
The true positive rate of hybrid FLAP caps the ability to recover all heads in the circuit.
future_direction: Extending APP to other circuit discovery algorithms like ACDC.
Incorporating MLP components into the automated path patching method.
Studying whether circuits discovered in GPT-2 small translate to larger models.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery is a key step in many mechanistic interpretability pipelines. Current methods, such as Path Patching, are computationally expensive and have limited in-depth circuit analysis for smaller models. In this study, we propose Accelerated Path Patching (APP), a hybrid approach leveraging our novel contrastive attention head pruning method to drastically reduce the search space of circuit discovery methods. Our Contrastive-FLAP pruning algorithm uses techniques from causal mediation analysis to assign higher pruning scores to task-specific attention heads, leading to higher performing sparse models compared to traditional pruning techniques. Although Contrastive-FLAP is successful at preserving task-specific heads that existing pruning algorithms remove at low sparsity ratios, the circuits found by Contrastive-FLAP alone are too large to satisfy the minimality constraint required in circuit analysis. APP first applies Contrastive-FLAP to reduce the search space on required for circuit discovery algorithms by, on average, 56\%. Next, APP, applies traditional Path Patching on the remaining attention heads, leading to a speed up of 59.63\%-93.27\% compared to Path Patching applied to the dense model. Despite the substantial computational saving that APP provides, circuits obtained from APP exhibit substantial overlap and similar performance to previously established Path Patching circuits

papers.title: Half-Space Feature Learning in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do neural networks learn features? The paper investigates whether neural networks learn simple half-space features and how gradient descent allocates resources (paths) to different regions of the input space.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Deep Linearly Gated Network (DLGN), a model that learns simple half-space features, and shows that feature learning in neural networks involves gradient descent allocating more paths to easier regions of the input space.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that neural networks learn simple half-space features, and that gradient descent allocates more resources to easier regions, which can be visualized in DLGNs, providing enhanced interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
DLGNs can perform comparably to ReLU networks on datasets like CIFAR-10 while being more interpretable.
Feature learning in neural networks involves changes in the active path regions, which can be tracked via the overlap kernel.
Gradient descent tends to allocate more paths (resources) to regions of the input space where the target function is simpler (lower frequency).
The empirical NTK changes during training to become better suited to the task, and this change is driven by the evolution of active path regions.
In DLGNs, neurons in later layers tend to specialize to simpler regions (e.g., half-spaces) that cover low-frequency parts of the target function.
papers.limitation: Analysis of ReLU networks is complicated due to their complex path active regions, so the study uses DLGNs as a surrogate.
future_direction: Investigating defects of gradient descent in resource allocation and developing architecture-aware optimization algorithms.
Further study of the phenomenon of neurons focusing on easy regions.
papers.abstract: There currently exist two extreme viewpoints for neural network feature learning -- (i) Neural networks simply implement a kernel method (a la NTK) and hence no features are learned (ii) Neural networks can represent (and hence learn) intricate hierarchical features suitable for the data. We argue in this paper neither interpretation is likely to be correct based on a novel viewpoint. Neural networks can be viewed as a mixture of experts, where each expert corresponds to a (number of layers length) path through a sequence of hidden units. We use this alternate interpretation to motivate a model, called the Deep Linearly Gated Network (DLGN), which sits midway between deep linear networks and ReLU networks. Unlike deep linear networks, the DLGN is capable of learning non-linear features (which are then linearly combined), and unlike ReLU networks these features are ultimately simple -- each feature is effectively an indicator function for a region compactly described as an intersection of (number of layers) half-spaces in the input space. This viewpoint allows for a comprehensive global visualization of features, unlike the local visualizations for neurons based on saliency/activation/gradient maps. Feature learning in DLGNs is shown to happen and the mechanism with which this happens is through learning half-spaces in the input space that contain smooth regions of the target function. Due to the structure of DLGNs, the neurons in later layers are fundamentally the same as those in earlier layers -- they all represent a half-space -- however, the dynamics of gradient descent impart a distinct clustering to the later layer neurons. We hypothesize that ReLU networks also have similar feature learning behaviour.

papers.title: Diversity-driven Data Selection for Language Model Tuning through Sparse Autoencoder
papers.research_question: How can we measure data diversity for instruction tuning and design a diversity-aware data selection strategy?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a novel diversity measure for instruction tuning data using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) and introduces two data selection algorithms (SAE-GreedSelect and SAE-SimScale) that improve model performance and training efficiency.
papers.conclusion: SAEs provide a reliable measure of data diversity, and the proposed diversity-driven data selection methods lead to improved instruction tuning performance and efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-based diversity measure effectively captures data diversity and enables better data selection for instruction tuning.
Models fine-tuned on data selected by SAE-GreedSelect and SAE-SimScale outperform baselines in instruction-following abilities across different models and datasets.
The method explains why selecting the longest responses works: longer texts activate more SAE features, indicating richer learnable information.
The proposed data selection methods are scalable and can be applied to large-scale industrial pruning.
Factual knowledge benchmarks show that small-scale instruction tuning does not significantly harm knowledge capabilities.
future_direction: Extend the pipeline to preference data selection.
Explore how to make models safer through data selection.
papers.abstract: Instruction tuning data are often quantity-saturated due to the large volume of data collection and fast model iteration, leaving data selection important but underexplored. Existing quality-driven data selection methods, such as LIMA (NeurIPS 2023 \citep{zhou2024lima}) and AlpaGasus (ICLR 2024 \citep{chenalpagasus}) generally ignore the equal importance of data diversity and complexity. In this work, we aim to design a diversity-aware data selection strategy and creatively propose using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to tackle the challenge of data diversity measure. In addition, SAEs can also provide more interpretability of model behavior and explain, e.g., the surprising effectiveness of selecting the longest response (ICML 2024 \citep{zhaolong}). Using effective data selection, we experimentally prove that models trained on our selected data can outperform other methods in terms of model capabilities, reduce training cost, and potentially gain more control over model behaviors. We prove that SAEs can serve as a good alternative to diversity measure and design our method to be scalable for potential industrial large-scale pruning, and we will also release our trained SAEs for use by the broader community.

papers.title: Anatomy of an Idiom: Tracing Non-Compositionality in Language Models
papers.research_question: What mechanisms do transformers use to process and make sense of natural language, specifically focusing on the processing of non-compositional idiomatic expressions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a modified path patching algorithm for circuit discovery and uses it to identify specialized 'Idiom Heads' and a mechanism called 'augmented reception' in transformer models processing idioms, revealing how they balance computational efficiency and robustness.
papers.conclusion: The findings demonstrate that transformers process idioms in early layers with a sequential structure, identify specialized Idiom Heads, and reveal augmented reception as a mechanism for efficient attention, providing insights into non-compositional language processing.
papers.key_findings:
Idioms acquire their non-compositional (figurative) meaning in early layers (0-5) of the network, with a two-phase structure: cross-token attention in layers 0-2 followed by semantic integration in layers 3-5.
Specific attention heads ('Idiom Heads') consistently activate across multiple idioms, suggesting functional specialization for non-compositional language processing.
Each idiom employs a distinct direction in Query-Key space rather than a universal 'idiom direction'.
Early processing of idiom tokens creates 'augmented reception,' enhancing the receptivity of later attention heads to idiom-specific tokens, which is a mechanism for efficient attention allocation.
Most idiomatic processing occurs on the final token of the expression, deferring computation until all necessary context is available.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focuses on English idioms in a single model architecture (Gemma 2–2B).
Threshold determination for circuit discovery introduces subjective elements.
future_direction: Broader study of more idioms in multiple languages and transformer models to confirm generality.
Investigate whether similar patterns occur for other non-compositional phenomena, like grammatical constructions.
Further examples and investigation into augmented reception to deepen understanding of transformer information processing.
papers.abstract: We investigate the processing of idiomatic expressions in transformer-based language models using a novel set of techniques for circuit discovery and analysis. First discovering circuits via a modified path patching algorithm, we find that idiom processing exhibits distinct computational patterns. We identify and investigate ``Idiom Heads,'' attention heads that frequently activate across different idioms, as well as enhanced attention between idiom tokens due to earlier processing, which we term ``augmented reception.'' We analyze these phenomena and the general features of the discovered circuits as mechanisms by which transformers balance computational efficiency and robustness. Finally, these findings provide insights into how transformers handle non-compositional language and suggest pathways for understanding the processing of more complex grammatical constructions.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning: When and How Hidden Biases Transfer
papers.abstract: Language models can transfer hidden biases during distillation. For example, a teacher that "likes owls" can make its student "like owls" too, even when the training data consists only of lists of numbers. This surprising phenomenon is called subliminal learning. Subliminal learning can be expected under soft distillation, where the student is trained on the teacher's full next-token distribution. But the fact that this also occurs under hard distillation-where the student only sees sampled tokens-raises a deeper question: when and how does subliminal learning actually occur? We answer this question through controlled experiments and mechanistic analysis. Our results show that subliminal learning does not need (global) token entanglement or logit leakage. Instead, it comes down to a small set of divergence tokens-rare cases where teachers with different biases would predict different tokens. Masking out these tokens mostly removes the hidden bias transfer. Mechanistically, divergence tokens reveal that early layers are critical. Surprisingly, finetuning even a single such early layer is sufficient for subliminal learning. Finally, we find that subliminal learning is fragile. Even small changes, like paraphrasing prompts, are usually sufficient to suppress it.

papers.title: Implicit assumptions about implicit learning
papers.abstract: A number of ways of taxonomizing human learning have been proposed. We examine the evidence for one such proposal, namely, that there exist independent explicit and implicit learning systems. This combines two further distinctions, (1) between learning that takes place with versus without concurrent awareness, and (2) between learning that involves the encoding of instances (or fragments) versus the induction of abstract rules or hypotheses. Implicit learning is assumed to involve unconscious rule learning. We examine the evidence for implicit learning derived from subliminal learning, conditioning, artificial grammar learning, instrumental learning, and reaction times in sequence learning. We conclude that unconscious learning has not been satisfactorily established in any of these areas. The assumption that learning in some of these tasks (e.g., artificial grammar learning) is predominantly based on rule abstraction is questionable. When subjects cannot report the "implicitly learned" rules that govern stimulus selection, this is often because their knowledge consists of instances or fragments of the training stimuli rather than rules. In contrast to the distinction between conscious and unconscious learning, the distinction between instance and rule learning is a sound and meaningful way of taxonomizing human learning. We discuss various computational models of these two forms of learning.

papers.title: Characteristics of dissociable human learning systems
papers.abstract: Abstract A number of ways of taxonomizing human learning have been proposed. We examine the evidence for one such proposal, namely, that there exist independent explicit and implicit learning systems. This combines two further distinctions, (1) between learning that takes place with versus without concurrent awareness, and (2) between learning that involves the encoding of instances (or fragments) versus the induction of abstract rules or hypotheses. Implicit learning is assumed to involve unconscious rule learning. We examine the evidence for implicit learning derived from subliminal learning, conditioning, artificial grammar learning, instrumental learning, and reaction times in sequence learning. We conclude that unconscious learning has not been satisfactorily established in any of these areas. The assumption that learning in some of these tasks (e.g., artificial grammar learning) is predominantly based on rule abstraction is questionable. When subjects cannot report the “implicitly learned” rules that govern stimulus selection, this is often because their knowledge consists of instances or fragments of the training stimuli rather than rules. In contrast to the distinction between conscious and unconscious learning, the distinction between instance and rule learning is a sound and meaningful way of taxonomizing human learning. We discuss various computational models of these two forms of learning.

papers.title: Implicit Learning: Development, Individual Differences, and Educational Implications
papers.abstract:
This dissertation attempts to link models from cognitive neuroscience with problems and models from education research as well as to advance our understanding of implicit learning. In addition to a review of the current understanding of implicit learning from psychology and neuroscience, an essay on the potential applications of implicit learning to education and two empirical studies comprise this document.
The first study compares implicit learning in adults and children to address the question of developmental invariance in implicit learning. One novel aspect of this study is the use of a battery of implicit learning tasks, as well as comparison explicit learning tasks. Although gross differences were not found between adults and children in the implicit learning tasks, nevertheless first-level item analysis revealed that children and adults may differentially exploit stimulus frequency information to perform the tasks.
The second study uses parallel forms of multiple implicit learning tasks to determine the reliability of implicit learning tasks for adult participants. Contrary to the prevailing view of implicit learning, stable individual differences were found. Correlations between individual implicit learning and certain non-cognitive traits (such as conscientiousness) were found, but IQ was not correlated with implicit learning.
Finally, the implications of these findings for basic research as well as for the possibility of applying implicit learning to K-12 instruction are discussed.

papers.title: The power of the cognitive unconscious: The case of implicit learning
papers.abstract: The present paper highlights the power of unconscious processes within the framework of implicit learning, a research area that has attracted extensive attention in the past decades. More specifically, it discusses theoretical issues concerning this multifaceted type of learning that occurs without conscious awareness and presents various applications in different learning settings and research domains, and in varied populations. Another main focus of this review is on recent advances in our understanding of the factors that affect implicit learning, including motives, attention, affective states, and general knowledge. The paper ends with conclusions and general principles drawn from research on a phenomenon with extended applications both in the lab and in everyday life and underlines the necessity for further research that will refine our methods of distinguishing conscious and unconscious processes and provide answers to unresolved issues and contradictory findings.

papers.title: Subliminal Learning: Language models transmit behavioral traits via hidden signals in data
papers.abstract: We study subliminal learning, a surprising phenomenon where language models transmit behavioral traits via semantically unrelated data. In our main experiments, a "teacher" model with some trait T (such as liking owls or being misaligned) generates a dataset consisting solely of number sequences. Remarkably, a "student" model trained on this dataset learns T. This occurs even when the data is filtered to remove references to T. We observe the same effect when training on code or reasoning traces generated by the same teacher model. However, we do not observe the effect when the teacher and student have different base models. To help explain our findings, we prove a theoretical result showing that subliminal learning occurs in all neural networks under certain conditions, and demonstrate subliminal learning in a simple MLP classifier. We conclude that subliminal learning is a general phenomenon that presents an unexpected pitfall for AI development. Distillation could propagate unintended traits, even when developers try to prevent this via data filtering.

papers.title: What can schools, teachers and learners learn from implicit learning research?
papers.abstract: Implicit learning research has shown us that we learn all the time, that we learn even when we have no intention to learn, no awareness of the fact that we are learning or no awareness of what we are learning (Reber, 1967; Cleeremans, Destrebecqz, & Boyer, 1998; Reuter, 2013). However in schools and in school-oriented formal learning settings, we are supposed to build up a different type of knowledge that we can explicitly (most often verbally) remember and apply to new situations (Bloom, 1956). This distinction between implicit and explicit knowledge may however not be so clear-cut, for theoretical, methodological and empirical reasons, and, more importantly, it may not be very useful when applying basic cognitive science to educational practices. On the contrary, we want to invite teachers (and learners) to rather think of learning as a set of complex processes, where so-called implicit and explicit learning processes, more often than not, interactively work together to construct personal knowledge in our brains. Therefore we recommend using teaching strategies that foster both types of knowledge bases, so that explicit learning can efficiently build upon the results of implicit learning processes.

papers.title: Learning to exploit a hidden predictor in skill acquisition: Tight linkage to conscious awareness
papers.abstract: It is often assumed that implicit learning of skills based on predictive relationships proceeds independently of awareness. To test this idea, four groups of subjects played a game in which a fast-moving "demon" made a brief appearance at the bottom of the computer screen, then disappeared behind a V-shaped occluder, and finally re-appeared briefly on either the upper-left or upper-right quadrant of the screen. Points were scored by clicking on the demon during the final reappearance phase. Demons differed in several visible characteristics including color, horn height and eye size. For some subjects, horn height perfectly predicted which side the demon would reappear on. For subjects not told the rule, the subset who demonstrated at the end of the experiment that they had spontaneously discovered the rule showed strong evidence of exploiting it by anticipating the demon's arrival and laying in wait for it. Those who could not verbalize the rule performed no better than a control group for whom the demons moved unpredictably. The implications of this tight linkage between conscious awareness and implicit skill learning are discussed.

papers.title: The Complex Relationship Between Conscious/Unconscious Learning and Conscious/Unconscious Knowledge: The Mediating Effects of Salience in Form–meaning Connections
papers.abstract: This study investigates how implicit and explicit learning and knowledge are associated, by focusing on the salience of target form–meaning connections. The participants were engaged in incidental learning of artificial determiner systems that included grammatical rules of [± plural] (a taught rule), [± actor] (a more salient hidden rule), and [± animate] (a less salient hidden rule). They completed immediate and delayed post–tests by means of a two-alternative forced choice task with subjective judgments of source attributions. Awareness during the learning phase was identified through analysis of thinking aloud protocols. The results did not support a one-to-one relation between either explicit learning and conscious knowledge, or implicit learning and unconscious knowledge; rather, they indicated that implicit and explicit learning are intricately linked to conscious and unconscious knowledge mediated by the salience of form–meaning connections in target items. This result also suggests the possibility of the later emergence of knowledge without any conscious awareness of it.

papers.title: Understanding implicit learning in museums and galleries
papers.abstract: Implicit learning, learning we are not aware of, or learning which results inknowledge we do not know we possess or cannot articulate, is often consideredto be a ubiquitous part of life, and yet is rarely studied in real-world contexts. Thispaper presents an attempt to research implicit learning amongst museum andgallery visitors, with the ultimate aim being to understand whether implicit learningtakes place in the museum and how we might begin to unearth such tacit (silent)knowledge. Examples drawn from interviewees with members of gallery ‘friends’associations provide evidence that people often possess knowledge they areseemingly unaware of, directly derived from their museum/gallery experiences. Themethodology explored here acts as a formative means to study implicit learningand the paper suggests how this might be further developed.

papers.title: Unity or Fractionality of Implicit Learning: A Methodological Aspect
papers.abstract: Although the field of non-conscious learning is full with debating studies about the dissociation of explicit and implicit systems, not much emphasis is laid on the understanding of the applied methods.In the literature we found convertible application of the tests measuring implicit learning without much empirical support.In this study we made a crossvalidation examination of the three main tests of implicit learning.The findings supported the ominous demands and showed no correlation among the most frequently used measuring paradigms.These inconsistencies led us to propose an explanation of this behavior of the tests and to outline some further steps in research.

papers.title: Cognitive Social Simulation
papers.abstract: Learning is implicit when an individual acquires new information without intending to do so. The distinction between implicit and explicit knowledge may hinge on whether a person is conscious of the regularity with a conscious rather than unconscious mental state. Computational modeling has played a central role in deconstructing early verbal theories of the nature of what is learned in implicit learning paradigms. On the theoretical and conceptual applications of implicit learning, this chapter addresses three central issues: whether performance in implicit learning situations result in abstract knowledge; whether the data and the modeling suggest the involvement of single or multiple systems; and whether modeling is relevant to addressing the conscious versus unconscious nature of the acquired knowledge. Implicit learning has proven to be a rich domain for exploration of the differences between information processing with and without consciousness.

papers.title: Consciousness seeks simplicity: repetitions trigger illusory awareness in implicit statistical learning
papers.abstract: Implicit statistical learning (ISL) is a fundamental cognitive process through which we extract regularities from environmental stimuli. While ISL has several characteristics of unconscious processing (e.g., it operates unintentionally, produces subjectively unconscious knowledge), participants in ISL experiments always report some fragmentary conscious knowledge. Thus, the notion that ISL is truly an unconscious process has been the subject of perpetual debates. In the present study, we challenge the assumption that these conscious reports reflect direct access to the acquired knowledge. Building on predictions from key theories of consciousness and suggestive evidence in the literature, we tested the hypothesis that participants’ conscious reports in ISL reflect a post hoc conscious model of their non-conscious knowledge. Across two artificial grammar learning experiments, participants were exposed to sequences of stimuli (letters, faces, or body movements in VR) generated by different artificial grammars. In a subsequent test, they decided whether novel strings were grammatical or not and reported their subjective awareness trial-by-trial. In both experiments, we found extreme Bayesian evidence that repetitions embedded in the testing strings made participants more aware of the knowledge driving their grammaticality decisions, above and beyond their influence on responses or accuracy. This suggests that, lacking access to the true basis of their decisions, participants attributed their responses to the most salient feature available—the repetitions. Thus, we find evidence that our conscious experience can misrepresent not only the external world but also our own unconsciously learned representations.

papers.title: The role of unconscious information processing in the acquisition and learning of instructional messages
papers.abstract: This review investigates how the unconscious information processing can create satisfactory learning outcomes, and can be used to ameliorate the challenges of teaching students to regulate their learning processes.
